problem_framing: Infrastructure as a jobs-and-equity question — who builds it and who benefits, framed by a labour/environment coalition
main_arguments: 1) BlueGreen Alliance unites the largest labour unions with influential environmental organisations, on the premise that Americans need not choose between a good job and a clean environment. 2) Presents infrastructure priorities building on its 'Making the Grade 2.0' platform. 3) On the grid, Congress should direct FERC to develop interregional planning requirements on regular triennial cycles using joint models, assumptions, benefit metrics and approval criteria, with regions dropping duplicate reviews. 4) Benefits must be steered to those most in need through hiring and procurement policy and workforce training. 5) Proposes accelerating storage deployment with $50 million annually.
specific_asks: 1) Direct FERC to implement interregional transmission planning on triennial cycles under congressional baseline standards. 2) Enhance and enforce hiring and procurement policies benefiting low-income communities, people of color and women. 3) Expand workforce training programs. 4) Fund energy storage advancement at $50 million annually.
position: Labour-environmental coalition: supports the bill with equity conditions on hiring, procurement and training
verbatim_quote: "It means enhancing and enforcing hiring and procurement policies that spur local job creation and benefit low-income communities, people of color, and women." | "Congress should direct FERC to develop and implement interregional planning requirements subject to baseline standards established by Congress"

hearing: "LIFT America: Modernizing Our Infrastructure for the Future" - H.R. 2741, the "Leading Infrastructure for Tomorrow's America Act"
problem_framing: Broadband funding as only as good as the map and the standard it buys — divide framed through mapping accuracy, speed floor and wholesale access
main_arguments: 1) Draws on nine years as FCC Commissioner and Acting Chairwoman and on field observation of broadband's transformative power, including a rural telehealth pilot that cut road miles and emergency room visits. 2) Too many Americans and rural communities remain disconnected; schools without adequate connections leave students on the wrong side of the divide, and off-grid rural health clinics force patients to drive hours or forgo specialised care. 3) The FCC's coverage maps are unreliable enough to be discarded: providers should have to show where they actually serve using subscription-based data, checked against third-party sources such as Microsoft's public broadband usage data. 4) If the money is being spent boldly, it should buy future-proof capacity, not the minimum.
specific_asks: 1) 'Go big and be bold' on the scale of investment. 2) Fix the National Broadband Availability Map before using it to determine eligible unserved areas, requiring subscription-based evidence and third-party cross-checks. 3) Invest in at least 1 Gigabit symmetrical, future-proof service, and weight upgradability positively. 4) Add a clause prohibiting funding recipients from unreasonably withholding wholesale service to other providers.
position: Former regulator: supports large-scale investment conditioned on better maps, a high speed standard and wholesale access obligations
verbatim_quote: "First, I recommend that you go big and be bold." | "To be frank, I recommend that we throw those coverage maps out." | "Accordingly, I recommend adding a clause to the legislation that prohibits recipients from unreasonably withholding wholesale service to other broadband providers."

hearing: "LIFT America: Modernizing Our Infrastructure for the Future" - H.R. 2741, the "Leading Infrastructure for Tomorrow's America Act"
problem_framing: Infrastructure from the cities' side — rejects the framing that urban authority must be traded away to serve rural areas
main_arguments: 1) Speaks for the US Conference of Mayors, representing mayors of more than 1,400 cities of 30,000 or more, as a five-term mayor of Piscataway, New Jersey. 2) Supports universal service efforts to make broadband available to urban constituents who cannot afford the price of service — locating affordability in cities, not only in rural areas. 3) The private sector's willingness to extend networks into low-income and disadvantaged neighbourhoods has been uneven. 4) Directly rejects what it calls the false narrative that diminishing or subordinating larger cities' property rights would translate into industry investment in rural America.
specific_asks: 1) Approve H.R. 2741 (the LIFT America Act). 2) Refuse the premise that subordinating cities' property rights will produce rural investment.
position: Municipal government association: supports the bill and defends local authority
verbatim_quote: "We urge the Committee to be a partner by approving HR 2741." | "Further, Congress can provide a service to all Americans by refusing to accept the false narrative that diminishing 3 or subordinating larger cities' property rights will somehow translate into industry investment in rural America with new state-of-the-art technologies." | "The private sector's willingness to extend networks into low-income and disadvantaged neighborhoods, however, has been uneven."

hearing: Small Businesses and Their Limitations Without Reliable Access to Rural Broadband Field Hearing
problem_framing: Rural connectivity as a household and small-business constraint — divide experienced as unusable service, not absence of service
main_arguments: 1) Family impact: daughters in school cannot upload easily, speeds drop and cut off, making school work frustrating and stressful. 2) Business impact as owner of a real estate brokerage of over 20 years: cannot upload photos to the MLS from a home office inside city limits, and since most paperwork is sent, signed and stored electronically, working from home is next to impossible. 3) Market effect: buyers now ask about internet before schools, so communities with better internet become more desirable and valuable. 4) Concludes good internet is no longer a luxury but a foundation of future growth.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt
position: Small business owner: supports rural broadband investment, framed through property values and workability
verbatim_quote: "Good internet is no longer a luxury Top notch internet is a foundation of future growth" | "First question used to be Schools now it's “What type of Internet is available ?”"

hearing: Small Businesses and Their Limitations Without Reliable Access to Rural Broadband Field Hearing
problem_framing: Rural broadband as a health-system crisis — connectivity as clinical infrastructure
main_arguments: 1) Speaks for the Isanti County Broadband Task Force together with Cambridge Medical Center and its 55 admitting physicians, Presbyterian Homes & Services, county public health and allied organisations, plus hundreds of nurses, technicians, aides and support staff. 2) States plainly that inadequate broadband has become a crisis in rural areas. 3) Routine activities of residents and businesses now require internet access. 4) Work-from-home and business-from-home activity is growing alongside technology-based health care, which makes business-class broadband availability the binding constraint.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt
position: Rural health and community coalition: supports expanding rural broadband access
verbatim_quote: "BACKGROUND The lack of adequa te broadband has become a crisis in rural areas." | "Work from home and business from home activities are increasing as are technology-based health care making business class broadband availabil[ity]"

organization: East Central Minnesota Educational Cable Cooperative
hearing: Small Businesses and Their Limitations Without Reliable Access to Rural Broadband Field Hearing
problem_framing: Rural broadband as a condition for business viability, workforce retention and educational equity at once
main_arguments: 1) Small businesses are the lifeblood of rural communities, and agriculture, tourism, hospitality, manufacturing, healthcare and retail all depend on the internet to reach suppliers and customers. 2) Those businesses also need an educated workforce willing to live and raise families in rural areas — connectivity is a residency decision, not only a business input. 3) Without affordable high-speed internet, businesses cannot thrive, families are less likely to locate there, and providing a fair and equitable education is difficult. 4) Notes the resignation of rural residents who are 'forced to get by and make due with what we have'.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt
position: Educational cable cooperative: supports affordable rural high-speed access, tying it to equitable education
verbatim_quote: "Without access to affordable high speed Internet, businesses cannot thrive, families are less likely to locate in the area and it is difficult to provide a fair and equitable education." | "Those of us who commit to life in a rural community are forced to get by and make due with what we have."

hearing: Small Businesses and Their Limitations Without Reliable Access to Rural Broadband Field Hearing
problem_framing: Rural connectivity as a lag of two decades — divide told through a manufacturer's personal account
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as a manufacturer who designs automated machines (a CNC plasma machine) and has run training over 700 times across the USA, including for deaf and quadriplegic customers. 2) Presents the internet as a unique gift of communication and the precondition for the business existing at all. 3) States that technology moved beyond rural areas twenty years ago — framing the gap as long-standing neglect rather than a recent problem.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt
position: Small manufacturer: supports rural broadband investment, argued from lived business experience
verbatim_quote: "The technology has moved beyond our rural areas 20 years ago." | "The place you are sitting at or standing on was only possible through use of the internet. A unique gift of communication between people."

hearing: "STELAR Review: Protecting Consumers in an Evolving Media Marketplace"
problem_framing: Video marketplace regulation as obsolete — the satellite compulsory licence framed as an unnecessary distortion
main_arguments: 1) Speaks for more than 1,300 full-power, free and local broadcast television stations. 2) Argues viewers get better access to local news, sports, weather and emergency information if the expiring STELAR provisions are allowed to sunset. 3) STELAR is unnecessary in the current marketplace. 4) The many program carriage agreements successfully concluded outside the broadcast-only framework show the regulatory structure does not justify reauthorisation.
specific_asks: Let STELAR expire at the end of the year, as Congress originally intended, rather than reauthorising it
position: Broadcast industry association: opposes STELAR reauthorisation
verbatim_quote: "Congress should allow STELAR to expire as it originally intended." | "The countless other program carriage agreements successfully completed outside this broadcast-only framework reveal that this regulatory structure simply does not justify STELAR's reauthorisation."

hearing: "STELAR Review: Protecting Consumers in an Evolving Media Marketplace"
problem_framing: Satellite licence as consumer protection and a building block of video competition — with open internet folded in as the adjacent fight
main_arguments: 1) 870,000 satellite subscribers should not be a bargaining chip in decades-long disputes between broadcasters and MVPDs. 2) Under all its names the law has ensured satellite companies can retransmit local broadcast stations to all customers, letting viewers in unserved areas keep a full range of national programming. 3) Failing to reauthorise would put already-achieved video competition at risk. 4) Retransmission consent could be improved with clear good-faith standards and prohibition of per se bad-faith conduct. 5) Extends the argument to broadband: discriminatory data caps and zero-rating may hold back online video competition, with risk compounded by vertical integration.
specific_asks: 1) Reauthorise STELAR, preferably making it permanent. 2) Adopt clear good-faith standards in retransmission consent and prohibit per se bad-faith actions. 3) Support strong open internet rules under Title II. 4) Examine whether discriminatory data caps and zero-rating restrain online video competition.
position: Public-interest advocacy: supports permanent reauthorisation and Title II open internet rules
verbatim_quote: "Congress must reauthorize STELAR or, even better, make it permanent. 870,000 satellite subscribers should not be a bargaining chip in the decades-long disputes between broadcasters and MVPDs." | "In addition to supporting strong open internet rules under Title II of the Communications Act, Congress should examine whether discriminatory data caps and zero-rating hold back online video competition"

hearing: "STELAR Review: Protecting Consumers in an Evolving Media Marketplace"
problem_framing: Video law renewal as an opportunity for broader market reform — with retransmission fees framed as crowding out rural broadband investment
main_arguments: 1) Speaks as the AT&T executive responsible for securing content rights from major networks and local station groups. 2) Consumers are driving revolutionary change in the video marketplace by demanding content where and how they want it. 3) The satellite distant-signal licence serves hundreds of thousands of rural homes left behind by broadcasters and cable providers; without it those largely rural subscribers lose network programming. 4) Retransmission fees are the fastest rising part of consumers' pay-TV bills, leaving MVPDs fewer resources for innovative offers, independent programming and expanding broadband into rural areas — connecting video regulation directly to the rural broadband gap.
specific_asks: 1) Renew STELAR, including the satellite distant-signal licence. 2) Make that licence permanent, as it already is for cable. 3) Use reauthorisation as the occasion for broader reform of the video marketplace.
position: Carrier/MVPD: supports renewal and permanence of the distant-signal licence plus wider reform
verbatim_quote: "Congress should take this opportunity to make permanent the satellite distant-signal license that brings network programming to these rural customers." | "As retransmission fees go up each year, which represent the fastest rising part of consumers' pay-TV bills, it leaves fewer resources for MVPDs to pay for things like innovative offers, independent programming and the expansion of broadband into rural areas."

hearing: "STELAR Review: Protecting Consumers in an Evolving Media Marketplace"
problem_framing: Retransmission consent as a direct drain on small rural operators' ability to fund broadband — video policy read as broadband policy
main_arguments: 1) Founded BOYCOM VISION, a small cable system in the Ozark Mountains, in 1992, and speaks also as Vice Chairman of ACA Connects. 2) Double-digit increases, blackouts and forced carriage of junk channels persist today. 3) Problems in the retransmission consent market have hindered upgrading broadband networks and deploying in the most rural areas — which contradicts bipartisan calls to solve the digital divide. 4) Capital access is itself a barrier: banks would not lend to small rural providers and RUS loans were unavailable to a cable operator, so the investment was financed by a second mortgage on the family home and farm. 5) These are exactly the rural places Congress says need help.
specific_asks: 1) Congress must act to improve conditions for rural customers of small operators. 2) Consider approaches such as the prior 'Local Choice' proposal. 3) Help with respect to buying groups.
position: Small rural cable operator: seeks retransmission consent reform as a precondition for rural broadband investment
verbatim_quote: "In the meantime, problems in the retransmission consent market have hindered us from upgrading our broadband networks and deploying in the most rural of areas, all of which contradicts constant bipartisan and bicameral calls for solving the digital divide." | "Because banks weren't eager to lend to small rural providers and getting Rural Utilities Service loans as a cable operator was impossible, we did it on our own, which meant taking out a second mortgage on our home and our farm as collateral for our capital investment."

hearing: Broadband Mapping: Small Carrier Perspectives on a Path Forward
problem_framing: Broadband mapping accuracy as the gatekeeper of rural funding — argued from an electric cooperative's position
main_arguments: 1) The cooperative serves rural communities investor-owned utilities bypassed because of sparse population — the same economics that now leave them off broadband maps. 2) Fewer than 10,000 electric consumer-members, 95% farmers and rural residential customers, across 2,508 miles of line. 3) Part of the broader electric cooperative industry represented by NRECA, serving one in eight Americans and covering 56% of the US landmass. 4) The costs of inaccurate mapping fall directly on farmers, ranchers, small businesses and residents — including those in 93 percent of the nation's persistent poverty counties.
specific_asks: More granular and accurate broadband mapping (the stated purpose of the testimony); no further discrete request captured in the excerpt
position: Rural electric cooperative: supports granular mapping so rural funding reaches actually-unserved locations
verbatim_quote: "ACEC provides electricity to rural communities that investor-owned utilities bypassed, in part due to our sparse population." | "These costs are borne directly by the farmers, ranchers, small businesses and other residents of the nation's rural communities – including those in 93 percent of the nation's persistent poverty counties."

hearing: Broadband Mapping: Small Carrier Perspectives on a Path Forward
problem_framing: Mapping method as the reason genuinely unserved rural locations are hidden from support programs
main_arguments: 1) Speaks for the Range Companies — a rural telephone cooperative and its subsidiaries serving Montana, Wyoming, Colorado and South Dakota — and as a board member of WTA, Advocates for Rural Broadband. 2) Like most small rural providers, it has very rural areas that are cost-prohibitive to serve at speeds comparable to denser areas. 3) An alternative mapping system tied to existing provider networks would properly identify outlying locations as unserved, so universal service support or broadband grants could be targeted where they are needed.
specific_asks: Adopt a mapping system better tied to existing provider networks so outlying unserved locations are correctly identified and can be targeted by universal service support or grants
position: Small rural carrier: supports mapping reform to redirect support to genuinely unserved locations
verbatim_quote: "Were an alternative mapping system used that was better tied to existing provider networks, the outlying locations could be properly identified as unserved so that universal service support or broadband grants could be targeted to the locations in need." | "But like most small, rural providers, we have very rural areas that are cost prohibitive to serve with speeds comparable to those that are available in more densely populated areas."

hearing: Broadband Mapping: Small Carrier Perspectives on a Path Forward
problem_framing: Overstated coverage data as the mechanism that misdirects federal funds away from rural carriers
main_arguments: 1) Speaks for CCA, whose members range from small rural providers with fewer than 5,000 customers to nationwide carriers. 2) The core need is coverage data that reliably reflects where service actually exists in rural America, so federal funds reach the carriers serving the most remote areas. 3) The FCC's own investigation should be used to understand and rectify overstated coverage figures. 4) Technical parameters drive the overstatement: cell edge probability should be raised to 90 percent or higher, as proposed by both nationwide and rural carriers. 5) Cell loading factor should be at least 50 percent on the downlink, reflecting that rural consumers are more likely to rely on mobile as their primary or only internet connection.
specific_asks: 1) Use the FCC investigation to correct overstated coverage figures and improve the next mobile data collection. 2) Adopt a cell edge probability of 90 percent or higher. 3) Adopt a cell loading factor of at least 50 percent on the downlink. 4) Revisit clutter factors.
position: Competitive carrier association: supports stricter mapping parameters to redirect federal support to genuinely unserved rural areas
verbatim_quote: "The FCC should use the investigation to understand and rectify overstated coverage figures, and take steps to improve the next mobile coverage data collection." | "The FCC should revisit this parameter and adopt a cell loading factor of at least 50 percent on the downlink, or higher, to reflect the reality that consumers in rural areas are more likely to rely on their mobile connection for their primary or only internet connection."

hearing: Broadband Mapping: Small Carrier Perspectives on a Path Forward
problem_framing: Mapping granularity balanced against reporting burden on very small rural providers
main_arguments: 1) Speaks from over 50 years in telecommunications for UniTel, a local rural provider founded in 1902, serving roughly 280 square miles across parts of 16 communities in three Maine counties. 2) Supports more granular broadband mapping as the subject of the hearing. 3) Frames the recommendations as striking a reasonable balance: more granular reporting is work for providers, but more granular reports also shrink the scope of challenge processes compared with today.
specific_asks: Adopt the more granular reporting recommendations described, balancing provider reporting burden against a narrower challenge process
position: Small rural carrier: supports granular mapping with attention to small-provider reporting burden
verbatim_quote: "These recommendations also strike a reasonable balance in terms of the work that providers will need to do in reporting more granular data while also minimizing the scope of challenge processes due to more granular reports than are available today."

hearing: "Building Opportunity in Rural America through Affordable, Reliable and High-Speed Broadband"
problem_framing: Tribal sovereignty and market failure — no return on investment means no carrier will ever come
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as an elected councilwoman of the sovereign Havasupai Nation and the Council's telecommunications lead. 2) The Tribe could not participate in online education opportunities until 2018, and children must leave the community for schooling. 3) The ruralness and population size mean there is no return on investment for outside ISPs or major telecoms to build the infrastructure — the gap is structural, not temporary. 4) MuralNet, a nonprofit, is what promised to help the community bridge the divide, in place of commercial providers.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt
position: Tribal government: supports tribal-controlled connectivity where commercial investment will not come
verbatim_quote: "The ruralness and population size of our community means there is no return on investment for outside Internet service providers or major telecoms to consider building the infrastructure." | "MuralNet had promised to help the community bridge the Digital Divide."

hearing: "Building Opportunity in Rural America through Affordable, Reliable and High-Speed Broadband"
problem_framing: Broadband as clinical infrastructure — connectivity framed through stroke mortality in the rural Southeast
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as Dean of the Medical College of Georgia on providing telestroke services to patients presenting at rural hospitals. 2) Georgia sits in the 'Stroke Belt', a region of high stroke incidence, and the centre serves rural southeastern Georgia and South Carolina — the 'buckle' of that belt. 3) Cites that nationwide 64% of US hospitals were not using TPA, positioning telemedicine as the mechanism for extending time-critical treatment. 4) References American Heart Association policy recommendations on implementing telemedicine within stroke systems of care.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt
position: Academic medicine: supports rural broadband as a precondition for telemedicine and stroke care
verbatim_quote: "I am here to recount my experiences as a physician providing telestroke services, a form of telemedicine, to stroke patients presenting at hospitals in the rural Southeastern United States." | "We are the Joint Commission certified Advanced Comprehensive Stroke Center that serves patients in rural southeastern Georgia and South Carolina, areas that are in the “buckle of the Stroke Belt”."

hearing: "Building Opportunity in Rural America through Affordable, Reliable and High-Speed Broadband"
problem_framing: Broadband as agricultural production infrastructure — precision agriculture makes connectivity a farm input
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as a corn, soybean and greenhouse farmer and President of Missouri Farm Bureau, on behalf of the American Farm Bureau Federation. 2) Rural broadband, both fixed and mobile, is essential to modern agriculture, to the farmers and ranchers who grow food, and to rural quality of life. 3) Transferring farm data — described as essential to the future success of every farmer — requires fast, reliable and affordable broadband, making the three attributes inseparable.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt
position: Agricultural federation: supports rural broadband investment as farm infrastructure
verbatim_quote: "Rural broadband (fixed and mobile) is essential to modern agriculture, the farmers and ranchers who grow our food and the quality of life for rural Americans." | "Transferring this data, which is essential to the future success of every farmer, requires access to fast reliable and affordable broadband."

hearing: "Building Opportunity in Rural America through Affordable, Reliable and High-Speed Broadband"
problem_framing: Broadband as rural economic development strategy — a leveller between urban and rural, but only with a talent strategy attached
main_arguments: 1) Speaks for Greater Bemidji, a public-private partnership with three staff and a $300,000 budget funded mostly by 70-plus regional businesses. 2) Broadband has the potential to level the playing field between urban and rural as never before in history. 3) Distinguishes between kinds of rural regions — the gap is not uniform. 4) Positions connectivity as the essential input to rural economic development rather than an amenity.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt
position: Regional economic development partnership: supports broadband as the basis of rural competitiveness
verbatim_quote: "Broadband has the potential to level the playing field between urban and rural as never before in history." | "One could even say that there are two kinds of rural regions in the US"

hearing: "Building Opportunity in Rural America through Affordable, Reliable and High-Speed Broadband"
problem_framing: Connectivity as necessary but not sufficient — rural competitiveness requires adoption and innovation capacity on top of the network
main_arguments: 1) Red Wing Ignite is the only rural city in US Ignite's network of 28 Smart Gigabit Communities. 2) US Ignite's role is to help communities expedite adoption of services and develop practices that stimulate job growth, startups and real estate investment — adoption, not just access. 3) To compete globally, rural communities need a different strategy: one that builds density of talent, people and resources to drive innovation. 4) Cites Minnesota's competitive grants to unserved or underserved communities aimed at the state's statutory goals of 100 Mbps down and 20 Mbps up by 2026.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a federal request — the excerpt describes the Minnesota state grant model and the adoption strategy as the approach to follow
position: Rural innovation intermediary: supports pairing broadband funding with adoption and talent-density strategy
verbatim_quote: "To be competitive in a global economy, rural communities require a different strategy - one that builds density of talent, people and resources to drive innovation." | "These grants are awarded on a competitive basis to unserved or underserved communities to help all of Minnesota reach the statutory speed goals of 100 Mbps down and 20 Mbps up by 2026."

hearing: "Our Wireless Future: Building A Comprehensive Approach to Spectrum Policy"
problem_framing: Spectrum policy as industrial and international competitiveness policy, with rural reach as a derived benefit
main_arguments: 1) NTIA advises the President on telecommunications and information policy, spanning spectrum management, broadband connectivity and the stability of the internet economy. 2) At the President's direction in 2018 the Department issued a report with 13 recommendations to improve the global competitiveness of the US space sector through spectrum policy. 3) A healthy satellite industry with sufficient spectrum access is essential to that competitiveness. 4) Among the recommendations is support for policies speeding satellite broadband delivery to both served and underserved areas. 5) Satellite integrates with 5G to help reach rural and remote areas where the economics of serving persist as a challenge. 6) NTIA also coordinates federal agencies for international spectrum negotiations, where the same bands matter for serving rural and less developed areas.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a request to Congress — the testimony reports the Administration's spectrum recommendations and NTIA's coordinating role
position: Federal agency: supports spectrum policies favouring satellite broadband and 5G integration for rural reach
verbatim_quote: "Among the recommendations made in the report is support of appropriate policies that can help speed the delivery of satellite broadband solutions to global markets in both served and underserved areas." | "This ties in well with the U.S. 5G push as satellite technologies will support, and integrate with, 5G networks, including helping to bring these services to rural and other remote areas where the economic challenges in serving these markets persist."

hearing: "Our Wireless Future: Building A Comprehensive Approach to Spectrum Policy"
problem_framing: Spectrum reallocation seen from public safety — 6 GHz as the backhaul that keeps rural 9-1-1 working
main_arguments: 1) Speaks for APCO, founded in 1935, the oldest and largest organisation of public safety communications professionals, with over 33,000 members who are mainly state and local employees running 9-1-1 centres, radio networks and emergency operations. 2) Public safety uses the 6 GHz band mainly as backhaul for 9-1-1 dispatch and first responder radio. 3) That use matters most in rural areas, where the alternative to microwave is prohibitively expensive or impractical fibre — if fibre is available at all.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a discrete request — the excerpt argues for protecting existing public safety use of the 6 GHz band
position: Public safety association: defends incumbent 6 GHz public safety backhaul, especially in rural areas
verbatim_quote: "Public safety uses the 6 GHz band mainly as backhaul for 9-1-1 dispatch and first responder radio communications, which is especially important in rural areas where the alternative to microwave would be prohibitively expensive or impractical fiber deployment, if it is even available."

hearing: "Our Wireless Future: Building A Comprehensive Approach to Spectrum Policy"
problem_framing: Spectrum management as a balancing exercise among competing demands, with rural coverage as one claim among several
main_arguments: 1) Speaks as Chief of the FCC's Office of Engineering and Technology after 45 years as an agency engineer, with recommendations based on sound engineering and efficient use of the airwaves. 2) The Commission is implementing a balanced policy responsive to demands for 5G, new satellite services, unlicensed use, advanced sharing and rural use. 3) Low-band spectrum matters particularly for coverage in rural areas. 4) The recent 2.5 GHz rule revision opens for 5G a band much of which lies fallow in rural areas, through greater incumbent flexibility, a priority window for Tribal Nations to obtain unassigned spectrum for their rural communities, and an auction.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt — a technical status report to the oversight committee rather than a legislative request
position: Federal regulator: presents balanced spectrum allocation, including a Tribal priority window and rural low-band coverage
verbatim_quote: "The Commission is hard at work implementing a balanced spectrum policy that is responsive to the many demands for spectrum access— for 5G, new satellite services, unlicensed, advanced spectrum sharing, rural use, and so forth." | "providing a priority window for Tribal Nations to obtain unassigned spectrum to address the communications needs in rural areas of their communities"

organization: Open Technology Institute at New America
hearing: "Our Wireless Future: Building A Comprehensive Approach to Spectrum Policy"
problem_framing: Spectrum as a public asset whose sale should finance broadband in underserved areas — reallocation framed as a distributive question
main_arguments: 1) Directs the Wireless Future Project at OTI, advocating universal, faster and more affordable wireless connectivity, competition and efficient spectrum use through unlicensed access and dynamic sharing; OTI belongs to the Public Interest Spectrum Coalition alongside consumer, civil rights, education, rural broadband and social justice organisations. 2) Warns the FCC is considering a 'private auction' that would violate the Communications Act and needlessly transfer billions in public assets to four foreign satellite companies that never paid for the airwaves. 3) Precedent exists: in 2012 Congress designated $7 billion of AWS-3 and 600 MHz auction proceeds to fund FirstNet. 4) Wi-Fi already makes access on smartphones and laptops faster and far more affordable, which is the case for unlicensed and shared use.
specific_asks: 1) Set aside $10 billion or more of C-band auction revenue to pay for broadband infrastructure in underserved areas. 2) Legislate, or at least urge, against the private-auction proposal to avoid unjust enrichment. 3) Require the FCC to authorise shared use of unused spectrum across the entire C-band, leaving technical interference rules to the agency. 4) Have the FCC and DOT solicit public input on alternatives such as the nearly vacant 4.9 GHz public safety band for vehicle safety applications.
position: Public-interest advocacy: opposes private auction, supports unlicensed/shared spectrum and earmarking auction proceeds for underserved-area broadband
verbatim_quote: "Just as Congress in 2012 designated $7 billion from the auctions of AWS-3 and 600 MHz spectrum to fund FirstNet, under your leadership Congress can set aside $10 billion or more of C-band auction revenue to pay for broadband infrastructure in underserved areas." | "the agency continues to consider proposals for a ‘private auction’ that would violate the Communications Act and needlessly transfer many billions of dollars in public assets to four foreign satellite companies that never paid for the public airwaves they use."

hearing: "Our Wireless Future: Building A Comprehensive Approach to Spectrum Policy"
problem_framing: Mid-band spectrum clearing as a speed-and-security race, with 5G presented as the instrument that closes the divide
main_arguments: 1) The US must act quickly to lead in 5G as countries compete to move beyond 4G; 5G promises speeds up to twenty times faster than 4G and an incremental $500 billion to the US economy. 2) 5G promises to close the digital divide by giving rural communities a meaningful alternative to fixed broadband. 3) Mid-band is the 'Goldilocks' band, balancing coverage and capacity across urban, suburban and rural America. 4) The C-band also supports government and public safety operations, provides links to remote and underserved areas, and keeps communications available in disasters when terrestrial services fail. 5) Transition is slow work: interconnecting fibre with 13,500 earth stations, 60 percent of them rural, takes substantial time.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a legislative request — the testimony defends the satellite operators' own clearing plan as the fastest and most secure route to mid-band availability
position: Satellite operator alliance: supports its private clearing plan for the C-band
verbatim_quote: "Meanwhile, 5G promises to close the digital divide by giving rural communities a meaningful alternative to fixed broadband services." | "Mid-band spectrum is the “Goldilocks” band for 5G, with the right balance of coverage and capacity to facilitate 5G adoption throughout urban, suburban, and rural America."

hearing: "Our Wireless Future: Building A Comprehensive Approach to Spectrum Policy"
problem_framing: Spectrum supply as the precondition for every claimed 5G benefit
main_arguments: 1) Speaks for CTIA and the US wireless industry, commending the Committee, Congress, the FCC and the Administration for identifying and repurposing spectrum for 5G. 2) Every expected benefit of 5G — economic growth, job creation, smart cities, improvements in public safety, health care and the environment — is predicated on spectrum availability. 3) Mid-band is valuable because it leverages both capacity and coverage: it handles 5G traffic and travels distances, which helps in rural and suburban settings.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a discrete request — the excerpt urges continued identification and repurposing of spectrum for 5G
position: Wireless industry association: supports making more spectrum, especially mid-band, available for 5G
verbatim_quote: "Every benefit that we expect to reap from 5G in the U.S. —economic g rowth, job creation, smart cities, and improvements in public safety, health care, and our environment —is predicated on the availability of spectrum." | "That's because it leverages both capacity and coverage opportunities—meaning it can handle the increased traffic that 5G will bring, and it can tr avel distances, which is helpful in more rural and suburban settings."

hearing: "Our Wireless Future: Building A Comprehensive Approach to Spectrum Policy"
problem_framing: Auction design as the determinant of whether rural carriers can compete for spectrum — without it rural America is left behind
main_arguments: 1) Speaks for CCA, whose members range from providers with fewer than 5,000 customers to nationwide carriers. 2) Without the right spectrum policies letting competitive carriers serve rural areas, rural America will be left behind, and every carrier must have a meaningful opportunity to access spectrum as it comes to market. 3) Wireless enables telemedicine and remote patient monitoring, increasing access to care particularly in rural areas. 4) On the C-band, argues the satellite alliance's proposed out-of-band emission limits would substantially harm 5G use, and agrees with AT&T that the Commission should seek further technical information.

hearing: "Legislating to Connect America: Improving the Nation’s Broadband Maps"

main_arguments: 1) Presents the Broadband Mapping Initiative and the Broadband Serviceable Location Fabric as foundational for availability reporting and therefore for closing the divide. 2) The pilot found that, among participating carriers, as many as 38% of additional rural locations are unserved in census blocks that today's FCC Form 477 approach would report as served. 3) The Fabric revealed that 48% of location counts in rural census blocks differ from current FCC estimates — the error is in the denominator, not only the coverage claim. 4) Frames the work as building an information ecosystem so agencies, policymakers and providers have the data to bring the unserved online.

hearing: "Legislating to Connect America: Improving the Nation’s Broadband Maps"
