specific_asks: 1) Repurpose 300 MHz of C-band for 5G using off-the-shelf compression. 2) Mandate multi-billion-dollar payments to the Treasury from an auction. 3) Provide financial incentives for US earth station operators to install compression equipment promptly. 4) Permit a private sector auction under FCC rules that fairly compensates all licensed satellite operators whose C-band rights are reduced.
position: Satellite operators outside the C-Band Alliance: support rapid clearing with Treasury payments and equitable compensation for all licensees
verbatim_quote: "Simply put, the FCC or Congress should: • Repurpose 300 MHz of C-band for 5G, which we believe can be done rapidly by using off-the-shelf compression technology. • Mandate multi-billion-dollar payments to the Treasury from an auction." | "Some have suggested that the FCC should simply evict all satellite operators from some or all of C-band to make room for 5G services."

hearing: "Repurposing the C-Band to Benefit All Americans"
problem_framing: C-band transition framed narrowly as a speed problem — which mechanism moves spectrum from one commercial use to another fastest
main_arguments: 1) Cisco produces technologies serving service providers, government and private enterprise, and its CEO has called 5G a 'step change' in networking that requires additional spectrum allocations. 2) The 3 GHz band should be opened as promptly as possible. 3) Has worked for several years on opening mid-band spectrum for terrestrial mobile services. 4) Took the early view that the private auction approach was faster than any other transition mechanism available to the FCC.
specific_asks: Open the 3 GHz band as promptly as possible, with the private auction approach considered as the fastest transition mechanism
position: Equipment industry: supports rapid mid-band clearing, favourable to the private auction approach
verbatim_quote: "Cisco believes the 3 GHz band should be opened as promptly as possible." | "Early on, we took the view that the private auction approach held promise as a faster mechanism than any other transition mechanism available to the FCC, and we urged its consideration."

hearing: "Repurposing the C-Band to Benefit All Americans"
problem_framing: Public airwaves as public property — the reallocation is an opportunity to fund deployment and digital inclusion, naming the Digital Equity Act
main_arguments: 1) Congress and the FCC must ensure the public's airwaves are used efficiently and in ways that best serve the public interest. 2) Public Knowledge has a long record on spectrum policy promoting public access, efficient use and pro-competitive policies so broadband is affordable and accessible for all, and belongs to the Public Interest Spectrum Coalition spanning consumer, civil rights, education, rural broadband and social justice organisations. 3) Supports reallocating portions of the C-band for wireless use, on a shared basis that protects incumbents. 4) Point-to-multipoint providers should be able to coordinate shared use in the upper C-band where satellite operators are repacked, plus opportunistic access to vacant lower-band frequencies until new licensees begin service — a route aimed at rural fixed wireless.
specific_asks: 1) Reallocate portions of the C-band for wireless broadband on a shared basis. 2) Permit P2MP coordination in the upper C-band and opportunistic access in the lower band. 3) Allocate auction revenues to deploy future-proof, high-speed fixed broadband in unserved and underserved communities and to fund digital inclusion and literacy initiatives like those in the Digital Equity Act (H.R. 4486 and S. 1167).
position: Public-interest advocacy: supports shared-use reallocation and earmarking proceeds for deployment and digital equity programs
verbatim_quote: "Congress should then allocate those revenues for the deployment of future-proof, high-speed, fixed broadband infrastructure in unserved and underserved communities, along with funding digital inclusion and digital literacy initiatives like those in the Digital Equity Act (H.R. 4486 and S. 1167)."

hearing: "Repurposing the C-Band to Benefit All Americans"
problem_framing: C-band as the only distribution path small rural cable operators have — clearing framed as a risk to rural video and broadband businesses
main_arguments: 1) ACA Connects represents more than 700 small and medium-sized independent providers of broadband, cable television and other communications services, deeply rooted in small towns and rural areas. 2) The issue matters especially to rural America because, while urban cable operators can receive programming over fibre as well as satellite, for most small and rural operators the C-band is the only viable option. 3) The broad geographic reach of C-band satellites lets programmers distribute feeds to thousands of earth stations at once, including in rural and remote areas.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a discrete request — the testimony argues that repurposing must protect small and rural operators' dependence on C-band reception
position: Small and rural operator association: supports repurposing conditioned on protecting rural earth-station reception
verbatim_quote: "And, while cable operators in urban areas can use fiber as well as satellites to receive this programming, for most of the small and rural cable operators that ACA Connects represents, the C-Band is the only viable option."

hearing: "Repurposing the C-Band to Benefit All Americans"
problem_framing: Spectrum auction as a public-revenue and government-accountability question — who runs the auction and where the money goes
main_arguments: 1) CAGW, founded in 1984 out of the Grace Commission, has more than a million members and claims $1.3 trillion in taxpayer savings over 35 years, positioning itself on efficiency and accountability. 2) Given the FCC's auction track record — which Commissioner Carr called 'a model for the world' — it is difficult to see why any entity other than the FCC should conduct the C-band auction, rather than a private sale. 3) The auction's potential value is between $11 billion and $60 billion depending on how much spectrum is sold and net proceeds after reimbursing relocation costs. 4) Senate appropriations report language points the same way, encouraging the FCC to prioritise spectrum that accelerates 5G deployment to rural communities.
specific_asks: 1) Only the FCC should conduct a public auction of the C-band spectrum. 2) Congress should authorise using proceeds — deposited in the Treasury — to deploy broadband throughout rural America.
position: Fiscal watchdog: opposes a private auction, supports an FCC public auction with proceeds to the Treasury and rural broadband
verbatim_quote: "Given this track record of success, it is difficult to see why any entity other than the FCC should be permitted to conduct the c-band spectrum auction." | "Proceeds from the sale of portions of c-band could be used for deploying broadband throughout rural America if Congress provides the authorization for such use, and auction revenues are deposited into the Treasury."

hearing: "Accountability and Oversight of the Federal Communications Commission"
problem_framing: Agency oversight report — supply chain security and public safety numbering, with rural carrier cost as a stated concern
main_arguments: 1) Reports on the Commission's agenda, including a rulemaking to establish 988 as a national three-digit number for suicide prevention. 2) On supply chain security, acknowledges the financial impact of requiring transition away from untrusted vendors falls hardest on small, rural carriers. 3) Proposes a reimbursement program to offset those transition costs — the mitigation is what makes the security requirement workable for small carriers.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a request to Congress — the statement reports proposed agency measures including the reimbursement program
position: Federal regulator: supports supply-chain restrictions paired with reimbursement for small rural carriers
verbatim_quote: "To mitigate the financial impact of this requirement, particularly on small, rural carriers, we proposed to establish a reimbursement program to help offset the cost of transitioning to more trusted vendors."

hearing: "Accountability and Oversight of the Federal Communications Commission"
problem_framing: Deregulatory infrastructure reform reported as working — measured by speeds, divide narrowing and rural build-out
main_arguments: 1) Reports that the Commission's reforms are delivering results: internet speeds up 56 percent in two years and the digital divide narrowed by about 20 percent. 2) The Commission has focused on ensuring rural America is not left out of the jobs, education and healthcare innovations built on 5G. 3) Cites the Rural Health Care Program's long-standing role and a proceeding providing up to $100 million for Connected Care pilots benefiting low-income patients, including Medicaid-eligible people and veterans. 4) Illustrates future applications with augmented reality glasses that anticipate user needs.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt — an oversight report on agency results rather than a legislative request
position: Federal regulator: presents deregulatory build-out policy as succeeding on divide metrics
verbatim_quote: "Internet speeds are now up 56 percent compared to just two years ago. The digital divide—the percentage of Americans that lack access to high-speed Internet services—narrowed by about 20 percent." | "That is why this Commission has focused on making sure that rural America is not left out of the jobs, education, and healthcare innovations built on 5G."

hearing: "Accountability and Oversight of the Federal Communications Commission"
problem_framing: 'Internet Inequality' — the divide reframed as hardening inequality that USF design should be redesigned to address
main_arguments: 1) Argues the persistent divide is hardening into a state of 'Internet Inequality', and the FCC must improve how it addresses this through Universal Service Fund programs. 2) Criticises the sequencing of the $16 billion, 10-year support decision: the Commission should have started with a smaller initial budget and shorter term while data and mapping are fixed — 'measure twice, cut once'. 3) Argues affordability should be a condition of subsidy, not an afterthought. 4) Illustrates the stakes through Duke University Hospital's telehealth program connecting Raleigh providers with rural North Carolina communities.
specific_asks: 1) The FCC should require USF auction winners to offer an affordable broadband service option. 2) Proceed with a smaller initial budget and shorter service term than $16 billion over 10 years until mapping and data are fixed.
position: Federal regulator in dissent: supports affordability conditions on universal service support and better data before large awards
verbatim_quote: "Quite simply, the FCC should require USF auction winners to offer an affordable broadband service option." | "today I want to talk about how the persistent problem of the digital divide is hardening into a state of “Internet Inequality,” and how the FCC needs to improve how it addresses this issue through its Universal Service Fund programs."

hearing: "Accountability and Oversight of the Federal Communications Commission"
problem_framing: Connectivity as a fair-shot precondition, with mid-band delay and Lifeline cuts named as the agency's concrete failures
main_arguments: 1) 'The future belongs to the connected': access to modern communications is needed for a fair shot at 21st century success, and clearing the way should be at the heart of the agency's work. 2) Not a single megahertz of mid-band spectrum has been auctioned for 5G despite consensus that the high-band-only focus cedes global leadership, creates 5G haves and have-nots, and leaves rural America behind. 3) Lifeline — the only program helping millions afford communications — has not been put on firm footing while a proposal to cut it by as much as 70 percent stands. 4) With less competition, rates rise and innovation falls. 5) Notes rules adopted to keep universal service funds from buying insecure network equipment, and urges using the equipment authorization process to build in security.
specific_asks: 1) Publish the expert staff's initial draft decision alongside the released decision. 2) End the proposal to cut Lifeline by as much as 70 percent and put the program on firm footing. 3) Auction mid-band spectrum for 5G. 4) Use each disaster to assess network resilience. 5) Use the equipment authorization process to encourage security by design.
position: Federal regulator in dissent: supports Lifeline, mid-band auctions, competition and agency transparency
verbatim_quote: "We have yet to auction a single megahertz of mid-band spectrum to support 5G service, despite overwhelming consensus that our early focus on holding high-band auction after high-band auction will cede leadership to our global peers, create communities of 5G haves and have-nots, and leave rural America behind." | "We have yet to put the only program that helps millions of Americans with affordable communications— Lifeline—on firm footing by ending the proposal to gut it by as much as 70 percent."

hearing: "Accountability and Oversight of the Federal Communications Commission"
problem_framing: Oversight statement focused on international spectrum negotiation rather than domestic broadband policy
main_arguments: 1) Reports back from nearly a week at the World Radiocommunication Conference 2019 in Sharm El-Sheikh, offering views on the event and its implications. 2) Credits the US delegation and the staff of the Commission's International Bureau. 3) Frames international spectrum outcomes as the relevant subject for the Subcommittee at this oversight hearing.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt
position: Federal regulator: reports on international spectrum negotiations; no domestic broadband position captured in the excerpt
verbatim_quote: "Just two weeks ago, I returned from spending nearly a week at the World Radiocommunication Conference 2019 (WRC-19) in Sharm El-Sheik, Egypt. I thought the Subcommittee might find it valuable if I took this opportunity to share my views about the event and its potential implications."

hearing: Business meeting to consider S.2204, to allow the Federal Communications Commission to carry out a pilot program under which voice service providers could block certain automated calls, S.2363, to amend the Communications Act of 1934 to establish a Telecommunications Workforce Development Advisory Council within the Federal Communications Commission, S.2381, to require review by the Government Accountability Office of screening protocols of the Transportation Security Administration relating to breast milk and formula, S.2638, to amend title 49, United State Code, to require small hub airports to construct areas for nursing mothers, S.2661, to amend the Communications Act of 1934 to designate 9-8-8 as the universal telephone number for the purpose of the national suicide prevention and mental health crisis hotline system operating through the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline and through the Veterans Crisis Line, S.2730, to establish and ensure an inclusive transparent Drone Advisory Committee, S.2786, to establish a Federal advisory committee to provide policy recommendations to the Secretary of Transportation on positioning the United States to take advantage of emerging opportunities for Arctic maritime transportation, S.2802, to amend the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 to reauthorize and modify the John H. Prescott Marine Mammal Rescue and Response Grant Program, S.2881, to require the Federal Communications Commission to make not less than 280 megahertz of spectrum available for terrestrial use, S.2898, to amend title 5, United States Code, to provide for a full annuity supplement for certain air traffic controllers, S.2909, to extend the authority of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration to enter into leases of non-excess property of the Administration, S.2964, to amend title 49, United States Code, to extend the authority of the Secretary of Transportation to issue non-premium aviation insurance, S.2979, to improve drug testing for transportation-related activities, and S.2981, to reauthorize and amend the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Commissioned Officer Corps Act of 2002; to be immediately followed by a hearing to examine the nomination of Thomas B. Chapman, of Maryland, to be a Member of the National Transportation Safety Board.
problem_framing: Not a broadband hearing — nomination testimony for the National Transportation Safety Board, captured because the Senate business meeting title referenced the FCC
main_arguments: 1) Appears as a nominee to the NTSB, introducing family and thanking the nominating senators. 2) The substantive exchange concerns the timeliness of NTSB investigation reports and how to accelerate them. 3) Argues that assumptions behind certification standards must be tested, referencing recommendations from the Lion Air accident. 4) Describes the 'most wanted list' as the Board's most important tool for leveraging priority recommendations, since the NTSB has no authority to compel them, and says members must work with legislators, Congress and local governments to get recommendations implemented.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a broadband-related request — the discussion concerns implementing NTSB safety recommendations
position: Nominee to a transportation safety agency; no broadband or telecommunications position — off-topic for the project's analytical frame
verbatim_quote: "The most wanted list, of course, is the most important tool that the NTSB has for leveraging its priority recommendations." | "It doesn't have the authority to compel these recommendations."

hearing: "Lifting Voices: Legislation to Promote Media Marketplace Diversity"
problem_framing: Media ownership and representation as a civil rights question — who is portrayed and who owns the outlets
main_arguments: 1) Founded in 1910, the National Urban League is a nonpartisan civil rights organisation dedicated to the economic empowerment of African Americans and other underserved populations, working through 90 affiliates across 36 states and DC. 2) Draws on the historical recommendation that African Americans be integrated 'into all aspects of televised presentations'. 3) That recommendation responded to African Americans not seeing themselves portrayed positively, nor seeing proper coverage of their issues or balanced perspectives in news and opinion — a diagnosis the witness carries into the current media marketplace.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt
position: Civil rights organisation: supports legislation promoting diversity in the media marketplace
verbatim_quote: "One of the most significant recommendations to emerge from the report was the integration of African-Americans “into all aspects of televised presentations.” This reflected the fact that African Americans did not see themselves portrayed in the media in a positive way and did not see proper coverage of our issues or balanced perspectives in news and opinion coverage."

organization: Santa Clara University School of Law
hearing: "Lifting Voices: Legislation to Promote Media Marketplace Diversity"
problem_framing: Media ownership diversity as a First Amendment and democratic-debate question, with broadcast framed as the lifeline of those inside the digital divide
main_arguments: 1) Diffusion of ownership and control of media has long been recognised by courts and Congress as a pillar of democratic debate serving the public interest, citing Associated Press v. United States on the widest possible dissemination from diverse and antagonistic sources. 2) For those living in the digital divide, and for millions of Americans, radio and television remain daily mainstays of news and public affairs — broadcast diversity matters most precisely to the unconnected. 3) Current policy does not fulfil the FCC's statutory mandate under 47 USC 309(j)(4)(d) to ensure small, women-owned, minority-owned businesses and rural telephone companies can participate in spectrum-based services.
specific_asks: Enact the legislation before the committee: adopt a tax certificate policy, require EEO data collection and reporting, require the FCC to study market entry barriers for socially disadvantaged individuals under 47 USC 257(b), and affirm the democratic value of media diversity
position: Legal academic: supports the media diversity bills, grounded in statutory and First Amendment obligations
verbatim_quote: "For those living in the digital divide, and for millions of Americans, radio and television broadcasting remain daily mainstays of news and public affairs information." | "Neither does it fulfill the FCC's 47 USC 309(j)(4)(d) mandate to ensure that small, women, and minority owned businesses and rural telephone companies are given the opportunity to participate in the provision of spectrum-based services."

hearing: "Lifting Voices: Legislation to Promote Media Marketplace Diversity"
problem_framing: Ownership diversity as a capital-access problem — training alone cannot produce minority station owners
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as founder and CEO of a broadcast ownership company of over 20 years, on behalf of NAB and its more than 7,500 local TV and radio members. 2) Local broadcasters connect and reflect diverse communities including women and communities of color. 3) The industry's Broadcast Leadership Training program cannot alone address the challenges of promoting diversity. 4) From conversations with program graduates, access to capital is the primary barrier to entry for new station owners. 5) The two main obstacles are finding equity and debt for smaller transactions, and locating a station with the positive cash flow banks require, since broadcast lending is not secured by tangible assets. 6) Offers a worked example: three years of effort to finance three Univision stations in Fort Myers-Naples, Minneapolis and Kansas City.
specific_asks: Congress should act legislatively to promote media diversity by addressing access to capital, which training programs alone cannot solve
position: Broadcast industry: supports legislative measures targeting capital access for new and minority station owners
verbatim_quote: "Based on countless conversations I have had with BLT graduates, access to capital remains the primary barrier to entry for new station owners." | "broadcast lending is not based on the value of tangible assets."

organization: Multicultural Media, Telecom and Internet Council
hearing: "Lifting Voices: Legislation to Promote Media Marketplace Diversity"
problem_framing: Ownership and employment diversity in media and telecom, explicitly linked to closing the digital divide
main_arguments: 1) MMTC, founded in 1986, is a national nonprofit dedicated to promoting ownership and employment diversity in the media, telecom and internet sectors. 2) Its work explicitly includes closing the digital divide and ensuring full digital inclusion for all, advocating before federal agencies and particularly the FCC. 3) Points to a concrete institutional win: on the 50th anniversary of the EEO Rule in July 2018, the FCC adopted the recommendation of 38 national minority organisations led by MMTC to move EEO staff from the Media Bureau to the Enforcement Bureau — relocating the rule from policy to enforcement.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a discrete legislative request — the testimony offers the organisation's views on the ownership and employment diversity bills
position: Multicultural media and telecom advocacy: supports ownership/employment diversity measures and digital inclusion
verbatim_quote: "We also work to close the digital divide and ensure full digital inclusion for all by advocating before federal agencies, particularly the Federal Communications Commission (FCC)." | "the FCC under Chairman Ajit Pai's leadership adopted the recommendation of 38 national minority organizations led by MMTC to move the FCC's EEO staff from the Media Bureau to the Enforcement Bureau."

hearing: "Empowering and Connecting Communities through Digital Equity and Internet Adoption"
problem_framing: Adoption as a demand-side and outdated-regulation problem — not supply and not price
main_arguments: 1) 'People adopt services, not networks': demand for broadband is derived, so policy should target demand rather than supply. 2) 16.2 million households are offline for lack of need or interest — a figure that grew over the past decade — against 6 million citing cost. 3) There is no single digital inclusion policy: needs and preferences differ and policy should let individuals express them. 4) The binding constraint is spectrum, especially mid-band/C-band, where 23 countries moved first.
specific_asks: 1) Congress should act on spectrum — authorize auctions, appropriate audit funds and enable agency reform. 2) Modernize statutes and regulatory structures the witness considers obsolete rather than reinforcing them.
position: Skeptical of further regulation; prioritizes market competition and spectrum release
verbatim_quote: "People adopt services, not networks." | "One area where Congress must act is spectrum, and only Congress has the power to the solve the problem."

organization: North Carolina Department of Information and Technology
hearing: "Empowering and Connecting Communities through Digital Equity and Internet Adoption"
problem_framing: Access and adoption as two sides of the same coin, from a state government perspective
main_arguments: 1) State policy treats adoption as a factor as important as physical access to the network. 2) People who adopt broadband are more likely to find jobs, learn new skills and navigate social services. 3) The institutional response was a governor's task force and an executive order directing state agencies to remove deployment obstacles and close the homework gap.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt — the extracted excerpt contains no request language; check the full PDF (22,200 characters)
position: Supports a holistic state-level approach combining infrastructure and adoption programs
verbatim_quote: "In North Carolina we recognize adoption as an equally important factor to addressing the digital divide." | "research demonstrates that individuals who adopt broadband are more likely to find jobs, learn new skills, and successfully navigate social services than those who do not adopt."

hearing: "Empowering and Connecting Communities through Digital Equity and Internet Adoption"
problem_framing: Digital equity as a redistributive commitment, at city scale
main_arguments: 1) Digital equity requires an honest assessment of what diverse populations need for meaningful participation — older adults, veterans, low-income families, people with disabilities. 2) For some communities the bottleneck is infrastructure, for others it is being able to subscribe to an affordable plan. 3) Local leaders are best placed to convene the relevant actors, yet cities like Detroit receive no federal funding for this work.
specific_asks: Examine the disparity between broadband usage and availability, and make recommendations to support localized adoption programs
position: Supports direct federal funding for municipal digital inclusion strategies
verbatim_quote: "Digital equity is a commitment for the least of us." | "I play a vital role in implementing digital equity initiatives for a city where one in four residents still do not have broadband access of any kind."

hearing: "Empowering and Connecting Communities through Digital Equity and Internet Adoption"
problem_framing: Digital inclusion / adoption — explicitly rejects framing the problem as rural infrastructure
main_arguments: 1) The divide will not close by filling rural infrastructure gaps alone: 14 million urban and 4 million rural households still lack any broadband subscription. 2) Income is the determining factor: households under $35,000 are 28% of all US households but 60% of those without broadband. 3) Digital inclusion work today means home service plus devices plus digital literacy training, delivered by nonprofits, libraries and local governments (NDIA's 400+ affiliates across 41 states).
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt — the extracted excerpt contains no request language; check the full PDF (7,477 characters)
position: Supports federal policy funding adoption and digital literacy, not deployment alone
verbatim_quote: "A mis-statement that we hear repeated often is that the digital divide would be bridged if we filled the broadband infrastructure gaps in rural areas." | "Households with incomes less than $35,000 make up 28% of all U.S. households but they account for 60% of those without any broadband internet service."

organization: Georgetown Law Institute for Technology Law and Policy
hearing: "Empowering and Connecting Communities through Digital Equity and Internet Adoption"
problem_framing: Affordability and lack of competition — adoption is flat despite availability
main_arguments: 1) Only 7% of the unconnected lack an available offer; 36% have access to 25/3 Mbps and either subscribe to a slower tier or go without. 2) Home adoption rates have been flat for three years — the problem will not fix itself. 3) There is no price transparency, so consumers cannot compare offers. 4) Barriers to competition (state bans on municipal networks, exclusive building contracts) keep prices high.
specific_asks: 1) Mandate that the FCC require providers to submit non-promotional pricing information and disclose fees and equipment costs. 2) Restore the Fixed Broadband Consumer Disclosure Label. 3) Prohibit states from blocking municipal networks. 4) Give a bidding preference to open access networks when allocating deployment subsidies. 5) Prohibit exclusive contracts with multi-tenant environments. 6) Strengthen Lifeline, expanding eligibility and benefit size.
position: Pro-regulation; supports municipal networks and a permanent low-income subsidy
verbatim_quote: "Congress should mandate that the FCC require broadband providers to submit non-promotional pricing information and should require public disclosure of added fees and equipment costs." | "First, Congress should prohibit states from blocking communities that wish to build their own broadband networks, be they municipal networks, public-private partnerships or other arrangements."

hearing: "Strengthening Communications Networks to Help Americans in Crisis"
problem_framing: Network resilience as an electric-power/communications coordination problem, argued from disaster restoration experience
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as Georgia Power's Distribution Support Manager, member of the FCC's Broadband Deployment Advisory Committee and its Disaster Response and Recovery working group, with nearly three decades in disaster response. 2) Draws on Southern Linc's performance across storms from Ivan and Katrina through Michael as guidance for improving wireless resilience. 3) Southern Linc's coverage spans extensive rural territory as well as metropolitan areas and highway corridors, and is widely used by state and local public safety agencies, school districts, rural local governments and utilities. 4) Identifies a concrete construction failure mode: fibre lines laid adjacent to electric poles.
specific_asks: 1) The FCC should evaluate construction practices for critical communications networks to ensure fibre lines are not laid adjacent to electric poles. 2) Congress and the FCC should formally affirm that ensuring interoperability between public safety communications systems and other wireless networks is a fundamental responsibility of FirstNet.
position: Electric utility: supports resilience measures and formal FirstNet interoperability obligations
verbatim_quote: "The FCC should evaluate construction practices for critical communications networks to ensure fiber lines are not laid adjacent to electric poles." | "Both Congress and the FCC should formally affirm that ensuring interoperability between public safety communications systems and other wireless networks is a fundamental responsibility of FirstNet."

hearing: "Strengthening Communications Networks to Help Americans in Crisis"
problem_framing: Communications resilience as a life-safety question, argued from the deadliest wildfire response
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as Fire Chief of Santa Rosa, the largest city and seat of Sonoma County, on the role of wireless communications and technology in public safety and emergencies. 2) Grounds the argument in the October 2017 fires that broke out across California's North Bay — at the time the worst wildfire in the state's history. 3) Speaks on behalf of the city's elected leadership, situating the ask as a municipal government position.
specific_asks: Support the RESILIENT Networks Act, introduced by Chairman Pallone and Rep. McNerney
position: Municipal fire service: supports the RESILIENT Networks Act
verbatim_quote: "This is why we support the RESLIENT Networks Act, introduced by Chairman Pallone and Rep." | "the City of Santa Rosa – the largest city in Sonoma County and the County seat – experienced, what was then, the worst wildfire in California's history."

hearing: "Strengthening Communications Networks to Help Americans in Crisis"
problem_framing: Next Generation 9-1-1 as a capital problem — the standards exist, the money does not
main_arguments: 1) NENA has over 16,000 members and is the leading professional association in the 9-1-1 space, developing standards, resources, education and certification. 2) The single most important action available to Congress is an immediate injection of capital into 9-1-1. 3) The sector is ready for it: industry and public safety spent over a decade developing the technical and operational standards, governance models and best practices for Next Generation 9-1-1. 4) Notes that emergency communications must be specialised by geography and hazard — wildfires, hurricanes, urban crime, and huge rural territories.
specific_asks: Give 9-1-1 an immediate injection of capital to deploy Next Generation 9-1-1, for which standards and governance models are already developed
position: Public safety association: supports federal funding for Next Generation 9-1-1
verbatim_quote: "That is why the most important thing Congress can do is to give 9-1-1 an immediate injection of capital. 9- 1-1 is ready for this injection: industry and public safety have worked together for over a decade to develop the technical and operational standards, governance models, and best practices for Next Generation 9-1-1."

organization: Free Press and Free Press Action
hearing: "Strengthening Communications Networks to Help Americans in Crisis"
problem_framing: Disaster resilience as an accountability failure — the agency has recommendations it has not acted on, with Puerto Rico as the case
main_arguments: 1) Frames the subject as the life-or-death issue of ensuring communications networks properly serve all people, especially in crisis, speaking for 1.4 million members including in Puerto Rico. 2) Draws on the aftermath of Hurricanes Irma and Maria. 3) After Hurricane Sandy the agency convened field hearings to inform resiliency recommendations, and the 2017 hurricane season report produced further recommendations — yet more than two years later the Commission has failed to heed even one of them. 4) Argues for learning from disasters in a timely way to improve emergency response and infrastructure recovery. 5) Notes the RESILIENT Networks Act would require the Commission to open a proceeding on the findings two years after enactment.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a single discrete request — the testimony presses for implementation of existing post-disaster recommendations and supports the RESILIENT Networks Act framework
position: Public-interest advocacy: critical of FCC inaction on resiliency recommendations, supports binding follow-through
verbatim_quote: "Yet even today, over two years later, the Commission has failed to heed even one of these important recommendations." | "I hope going forward we can make a greater effort to learn from disasters in a timely way, so we can do more to improve emergency response and infrastructure recovery."

hearing: "Strengthening Communications Networks to Help Americans in Crisis"
problem_framing: Resilience as industry-led coordination — voluntary frameworks presented as the working model to be codified, not replaced
main_arguments: 1) Speaks for CTIA and the US wireless industry on public safety communications as the frequency and scope of disasters increase. 2) Endorses the goals of the RESILIENT Networks Act, highlighting that it acknowledges the role of reasonable roaming agreements in maintaining continuity of service during emergencies — a principle already embraced in the industry's voluntary Cooperative Framework. 3) Supports the bill's focus on enhanced information sharing across industries, levels of government and the public safety community. 4) Since the Cooperative Framework's adoption, providers have worked with the FCC to expand the cell site data shared with consumers and local public safety officials.
specific_asks: 1) Support the goals of the RESILIENT Networks Act (H.R. 5926). 2) Support the READI Act (H.R. 4856). 3) Support the FIRST RESPONDER Act (H.R. 5928), on the basis that reliable 9-1-1 is the centerpiece of emergency communications.
position: Wireless industry association: supports the resilience bills, anchored on the voluntary Cooperative Framework
verbatim_quote: "We support the goals of Chairman Pallone and Representative McNern ey's RESILIENT Networks Act (H.R. 5926)." | "Second, the bill acknowledges the important role that reasonable roaming agreements play during times of emergency in ensuring continuity of service—a principle we support and have embraced in the Cooperative Framework ."

hearing: "Strengthening Communications Networks to Help Americans in Crisis"
problem_framing: Crisis-line access as public health infrastructure — the three-digit code framed as a suicide prevention measure
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as CEO of Behavioral Health Link, which runs a community-based call centre hub and mobile outreach, and COO of RI International, together offering a full continuum of crisis services. 2) Cites the FCC's August 2019 report to Congress: more than 47,000 Americans died by suicide in 2017 and more than 1.4 million adults attempted suicide, with suicide rising in 49 of 50 states between 1999 and 2016, by more than 20 percent in over half of them. 3) Endorses the report's conclusion that the Commission should open a rulemaking to designate 988 as the three-digit code, saying front-line crisis providers could not agree more.
specific_asks: Move H.R. 4194, the National Suicide Hotline Designation Act, as quickly as possible, incorporating the witness's three stated tenets
position: Crisis services provider: supports designating 988 and enacting the National Suicide Hotline Designation Act
verbatim_quote: "We conclude that the Commission should initiate a rulemaking proceeding through a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to consider designating 988 as the 3-digit dialing code for a national suicide prevention and mental health crisis hotline.” As front line providers of crisis services, we couldn't agree more."

hearing: Hearings to examine the state of United States spectrum policy.
problem_framing: Spectrum sharing as an engineering and process question, with federal-commercial coordination machinery as the subject
main_arguments: 1) CommScope is a leading US developer and manufacturer of wireless network equipment supplying the building blocks carriers and enterprises use for next generation networks. 2) Its customers span small rural wireless carriers and rural WISPs providing critical communications during COVID through to nationwide cable operators and utilities. 3) Describes how CSMAC working groups, organised under the Federal Advisory Committee Act since 2004, produced sharing, transition and relocation recommendations that shaped the AWS-3 rulemaking. 4) For the 6 GHz band, the FCC encouraged a multistakeholder group to operationalise the Automated Frequency Coordination system and address interference.

organization: Open Technology Institute at New America
hearing: Hearings to examine the state of United States spectrum policy.
problem_framing: Spectrum scarcity as a policy artefact — sharing can create abundance, and Wi-Fi is framed as the affordable route for places carriers will not build
main_arguments: 1) The pandemic reinforced that high-capacity and affordable connectivity are essential for working, learning and living at home. 2) Surging demand suggests scarcity, but smart policy can unlock abundant bandwidth by authorising dynamic sharing in more underutilised bands. 3) As a default rule, sharing puts vacant spectrum to use in rural, tribal and other underserved areas where it is needed most. 4) Credits the FCC for shared access across the entire 6 GHz band, which lets next-generation Wi-Fi accelerate availability and affordability of applications like telehealth. 5) Gigabit Wi-Fi 6 will quickly benefit homes, businesses and schools including in rural, small town and less affluent areas unlikely to see carrier 5G build-out for many years — the equity argument for unlicensed.
specific_asks: 1) Relocate auto safety applications to the nearly vacant 4.9 GHz public safety band to clear a contiguous Wi-Fi band. 2) The FCC or Congress should immediately extend the tribal priority window for vacant 2.5 GHz spectrum due to expire August 3. 3) Update and enhance the NTIA-FCC coordination MOU, with deeper engagement from OSTP and NEC.
position: Public-interest advocacy: supports dynamic sharing, unlicensed Wi-Fi expansion and extending tribal spectrum access
verbatim_quote: "Enabling gigabit fast Wi-Fi 6 will quickly benefit all homes, businesses, and schools, including in rural small town and less affluent areas that are unlikely to see mobile carrier 5G build-out for many years." | "And finally, the FCC or Congress should immediately extend the tribal priority window for access to vacant 2.5 gigahertz spectrum set to expire August 3."

hearing: Hearings to examine the state of United States spectrum policy.
problem_framing: Spectrum as property — federal spectrum management framed as a 98-year-old institutional failure, with 5G as the fastest route to close the divide
main_arguments: 1) Commercial spectrum reforms driven by the Committee — flexible use, competitive bidding, repackaging, dynamic sharing — became models worldwide and underpin a trillion-dollar wireless economy. 2) Federal spectrum, managed by NTIA and IRAC (founded 1922), has been governed essentially unchanged for 98 years and is due for review. 3) Invokes Coase: the 'first best' realisation is to liberalise the underlying resource by privatising spectrum itself, not merely the licensing regime. 4) With 100 million schoolchildren facing distance learning, policy still struggles to allow purchase of mid-band rights that would serve them. 5) Frames 5G as the quickest way to equalise the urban-rural divide, offering connectivity equal or superior to wireline fibre, while the US fights China 'on scraps of mid-band spectrum'.
specific_asks: 1) Liberalise and ultimately privatise spectrum rights rather than only the use and licensing regime. 2) Failing that, reform IRAC so the American people are represented and its decisions are accountable. 3) Free mid-band spectrum for 5G.
position: Academic/market-liberal: supports spectrum privatisation, IRAC reform and rapid mid-band release, framing 5G as the divide solution
verbatim_quote: "The first best realization of Coase's recommendation is to liberalize the underlying resource, privatize the spectrum itself." | "5G is the quickest way to equalize the digital divide between urban and rural America, providing the same, if not, superior connectivity than wireline fiber networks."

hearing: Hearings to examine the state of United States spectrum policy.
problem_framing: Mid-band clearing as the unfinished task — sharing treated as second best to exclusive licensed use
main_arguments: 1) Thanks the Committee and FCC for pandemic leadership that let providers respond dynamically to customers. 2) Points to the record: the FCC auctioned more spectrum in the last five years than in any previous comparable period, netting $67 billion for the Treasury, including the first incentive auction and the first high-band auctions. 3) Mid-band is suited to higher speeds and improved latency, particularly in more rural areas, and there is growing global consensus it should be allocated for 5G. 4) On the band NTIA studied for sharing, urges examining the potential to clear rather than share as much as possible — the clearest statement of the licensed-exclusive preference.
specific_asks: 1) Support the legislation making federal spectrum management more efficient. 2) Urge NTIA to examine clearing — rather than sharing — as much of the band as possible.
position: Wireless industry association: supports exclusive licensed mid-band clearing over shared use
verbatim_quote: "NTIA's recent report sought to evaluate whether commercial and government operators can share this band, but we urge NTIA to examine the potential to clear--rather than share--as much of this band as possible." | "Mid-band spectrum is perfectly suited to deliver higher speeds and improved latency, particularly in more rural areas."

main_arguments: 1) Testifies as a Captain with 24 years in the Pennington County Sheriff's Office, having served as patrol officer and eight years in the narcotics unit as investigator, undercover operative and supervisor. 2) Describes a county spanning the Black Hills, Badlands National Park, Ellsworth Air Force Base and Mount Rushmore — a large, sparsely populated area where coverage is the operational question. 3) Appears to give the field-level evaluation of FirstNet's progress.

hearing: Hearings to examine an evaluation of FirstNet's progress.
problem_framing: FirstNet as the post-9/11 answer to interoperability failure — and as proof that spectrum can be deployed fast
main_arguments: 1) FirstNet is the nation's only dedicated interoperable broadband network built for public safety, created by Congress in 2012 after the 9/11 Commission found first responders could not communicate seamlessly. 2) Public safety specified that the network be affordable, reliable, interoperable and custom-built. 3) It had to work both in urban canyons with Z-axis geolocation and in-building dead zones, and in the most rural parts of the country where no business case previously existed to build networks for public safety alone. 4) Deployment speed is offered as evidence: against CTIA's finding that reallocating spectrum for wireless use takes 13 years on average, FirstNet did it in six. 5) The FCC's Technical Advisory Board for First Responder Interoperability set the network's minimum technical requirements.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt — a progress report to the oversight subcommittee rather than a legislative request
position: Federal authority: reports FirstNet deployment progress, emphasising rural coverage where no commercial business case existed
verbatim_quote: "The network solution needed to be designed to work in the most urban areas, where network challenges come in the form of urban canyons, Z- axis geolocation,\5\ and in-building coverage dead zones; and in the most rural parts of our country, where previously, the business case did not exist to build networks just for public safety use."

hearing: Hearings to examine an evaluation of FirstNet's progress.
problem_framing: Public safety network build-out as a carrier commitment, with rural expansion presented as a top priority
main_arguments: 1) Reports on FirstNet's role connecting first responders through the COVID-19 pandemic, hurricanes and wildfires alongside daily public safety activity. 2) Claims delivery on Congress's vision of a single dedicated nationwide public safety network, now available in all 50 states, DC and five territories — up from five states opting in at the previous appearance. 3) Recalls that Congress created FirstNet after 9/11 on the Commission's recommendation because responders frequently could not communicate during emergencies. 4) States that reaching rural and remote America is a top priority, with over 1,000 new purpose-built FirstNet sites planned in the initial nationwide expansion, most of them rural.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt — a progress update to the subcommittee rather than a legislative request
position: Carrier operating the public safety network: reports progress and commits to rural site build-out
verbatim_quote: "Over 1,000 new purpose- built FirstNet sites are currently planned as part of the initial nationwide FirstNet network expansion, most of those in rural areas." | "Finally, I want to emphasize that reaching rural parts of America is one of our top priorities."

hearing: Hearings to examine an evaluation of FirstNet's progress.
problem_framing: The 9-1-1 centre as the missing link in the first responder network — data flow from ECCs framed as the next improvement
main_arguments: 1) Directs Washington DC's Office of Unified Communications, the city's 9-1-1 and 3-1-1 Emergency Communications Center, and speaks representing over 6,500 ECCs nationally. 2) Discloses appointment to the FirstNet Authority Board in October 2019 while testifying only in the DC 9-1-1 Director capacity — an explicit conflict disclosure. 3) Argues richer and potentially real-time information passed from ECC Next Generation systems into FirstNet would be a critical improvement, letting responders be better informed and operate more safely in big cities, small ones and rural communities. 4) The pandemic reinforced the need for rural coverage and capabilities, described as a foundational element of FirstNet.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a discrete request — the testimony thanks the committee for broadband expansion efforts, particularly the Streamline Act, and argues for ECC-to-FirstNet data integration
position: Municipal 9-1-1 authority: supports integrating Next Generation 9-1-1 data with FirstNet and expanding rural coverage
verbatim_quote: "Richer and potentially real-time information shared with first responders from ECCs Next Gen systems to FirstNet will be a critical improvement that can ensure they are better informed and operate more safely in big cities, small ones, and rural communities."

hearing: “Connecting America:  Broadband Solutions to Pandemic Problems”
problem_framing: Digital equity in K-12 — the pandemic exposed a home-connectivity gap that E-rate does not reach
main_arguments: 1) Frames the current challenge against two decades of progress: when E-rate was established in 1996 the FCC reported only 14% of K-12 classrooms had internet access. 2) The needs of the underserved grew exponentially during the pandemic, when devices and Wi-Fi-dependent remote services became essential. 3) Many Kansas teachers live in rural areas and could not teach without adequate broadband at home — the gap affected staff as well as students. 4) The district's workarounds show the limits of ad hoc fixes: hotspot locations worked for secondary students but not for families with primary-age children who could not travel independently, and maps of Wi-Fi-equipped shops revealed that rural and high-poverty areas had fewer access points. 5) The district paid for home internet out of CARES Act funding.
specific_asks: 1) Fund E-rate support for emergency connections and devices for schools, libraries and Native American communities. 2) Act quickly to provide communications and telehealth aid to the communities that need it most. 3) Make a strong investment in connectivity across communities.
position: Public school district: supports federal funding for home connectivity and devices, framed explicitly as digital equity
verbatim_quote: "With your support and commitment to equity, I urge you to make a strong investment in the future of our students, and ultimately in the future of our economy, as we strengthen the connectivity across communities." | "Many of our teachers live in rural areas in Kansas and were unable to teach without adequate or reliable broadband services from home."

hearing: “Connecting America:  Broadband Solutions to Pandemic Problems”
problem_framing: Market failure — the private sector has not closed the divide, and the New Deal electrification analogy sets the federal role
main_arguments: 1) CWA represents workers across telecommunications including more than 150,000 in wireline and wireless. 2) States the diagnosis plainly: the private sector alone has failed to close the digital divide, and as with 1930s electrification the federal government has a critical role in both access and adoption. 3) For years the union protested as major telecom companies let networks deteriorate and declined to upgrade low-income communities to fibre — an explicit claim of discriminatory investment. 4) The union urged regulators to reverse the growing divide, and argues that had its recommendations been enacted the current situation would be less severe. 5) Warns members to be skeptical of industry claims.
specific_asks: 1) The FCC should rescind its 2018 Small Cell Order and support local governments' role in facilitating safe wireless deployment. 2) The Commission should explore broadening the USF funding base to include broadband customers.
position: Labour union: supports federal public investment, local government authority and expanded USF contribution base
verbatim_quote: "This starts with recognizing the problem: the private sector alone has failed to close the digital divide." | "As with electrification in the 1930s, the federal government has a critical role to play in closing the gaps in both access and adoption." | "For years, we have protested as major telecom companies allowed their networks to deteriorate and failed to upgrade low-income communities to fiber-optic service."

organization: The George Washington University School of Law
hearing: “Fanning the Flames: Disinformation and Extremism in the Media”
problem_framing: Disinformation policy as a First Amendment risk — the danger framed as government pressure on speech and press
main_arguments: 1) Notes the subject is heavily laden with political passions and agendas, and that in 'our age of rage' every issue becomes associated with one party or personality, turning rights into functional questions. 2) Argues that abandoning bright-line protections for free speech and free press carries costs that must be weighed against the harms being addressed. 3) Proposes an alternative federal role: publishing data and information so citizens can reach their own conclusions, rather than regulating content.

main_arguments: 1) Co-founded the grassroots non-profit Marked By COVID on the day she buried her father, who died of COVID-19 on 30 June 2020 at 65. 2) Testifies on disinformation in the media from the position of a survivor rather than an expert. 3) Carries forward the two themes of her Democratic National Convention remarks: the existence of 'two Americas', one for the elite and one for everyone else, and that her father's only pre-existing condition was trusting the President.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt

hearing: “Fanning the Flames: Disinformation and Extremism in the Media”
problem_framing: Disinformation as a failure of media accountability, not a case for regulation — with local news decline as the structural backdrop
main_arguments: 1) Opens with a documented case: a 2005 Lou Dobbs segment claiming 7,000 new US leprosy cases in three years, when official statistics showed roughly 7,000 over thirty years. 2) The point is institutional, not individual: a mainstream journalist with a prime-time show lied, was publicly debunked on 60 Minutes, and prospered anyway, celebrated by executives for tackling 'hot topics'. 3) Situates the problem against the local press landscape: about half of the country's remaining 6,700-plus papers — roughly 1,250 dailies and 5,500 weeklies — are in small and rural communities. 4) Draws the constitutional line explicitly while identifying a legitimate congressional role.
specific_asks: Congress should shed light on how irresponsible media contributes to disinformation and its consequences for democracy, rather than regulating journalism
position: Journalist: opposes regulation of journalism, supports congressional scrutiny and transparency
verbatim_quote: "Congress can't, and shouldn't, regulate journalism in defiance of the First Amendment." | "What Congress can do is shed light on how irresponsible media contributes to disinformation in ways that have consequences for democracy."

hearing: Hearings to examine recent Federal actions to expand broadband.
problem_framing: Rural broadband as a planning failure — calls for a new national rural broadband plan built on five elements, with subsidy capture as the diagnosis
main_arguments: 1) Argues for a new national rural broadband plan incorporating the '5 M's of Successful Rural Broadband Deployment': Meaning, Money, Mapping, Municipalities and Management. 2) Diagnoses the historical failure: when the Universal Service Fund High-Cost Program became the Connect America Fund at the National Broadband Plan's recommendation, funding was simply given to the ten largest 'price cap' carriers rather than distributed by competitive auction. 3) Contributes an alternative data approach, asking counties to self-report their level of connectivity rather than relying on provider filings. 4) Welcomes the $3.2 billion Emergency Broadband Benefit in the Consolidated Appropriations Act and the $7.1 billion for schools in the American Rescue Plan. 5) Explicitly welcomes the reintroduction of the Accessible, Affordable Internet for All Act — one of the project's anchor bills.
specific_asks: Develop a decisive and coherent new national rural broadband plan organised around meaning, money, mapping, municipalities and management
position: Academic: supports a coordinated national rural plan, municipal participation and competitive rather than incumbent-directed subsidy
verbatim_quote: "Today, I will argue for a new national rural broadband plan, one that incorporates what I called in my written testimony, The 5 M's of Successful Rural Broadband Deployment: Meaning, Money, Mapping, Municipalities, and Management." | "funding was simply given to the 10 largest providers, known as ``price cap'' carriers, rather than distributed through a competitive auction."

hearing: Hearings to examine recent Federal actions to expand broadband.
problem_framing: Definition of 'unserved' as the decisive variable — a broad definition would divert money to easier areas
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as a former FCC Commissioner, noting for the record that he currently represents no party involved in the hearing's issues. 2) Argues the number of unserved households has shrunk precipitously, so the scale of the remaining problem is smaller than assumed. 3) Warns about definitional drift: if standards are set broadly, a great deal of the country will be deemed unserved, funding will flow to the easier areas and the genuinely unserved will be ignored again — the same targeting argument he made at the FCC. 4) Credits the agency's record: modernising the Connect America Fund, removing obstacles to rate-of-return providers offering standalone service, model-based support, reverse auctions and the Rural Digital Opportunity Fund Phase I.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a discrete request — the testimony argues for a narrow definition of 'unserved' so funding reaches the hardest areas first
position: Former regulator: supports narrow targeting of broadband subsidy, sceptical of expansive unserved definitions
verbatim_quote: "Ultimately, it means a great deal of the country will be deemed unserved. Funding will flow to the easier areas and the unserved areas will be, essentially, ignored again." | "Simply put, the numbers of unserved households have shrunk precipitously."

hearing: Hearings to examine recent Federal actions to expand broadband.
problem_framing: Closing the deployment gap as a costed, coordinated programme — the $80 billion figure plus intergovernmental coordination
main_arguments: 1) Speaks as a Quadra Partners co-founder who previously headed two large FCC bureaus and spent 18 months working with a group of RDOF participants, bringing lessons from that process. 2) Anchors the discussion on one number: the FCC's early-2017 staff analysis answering what investment would be required to close the deployment gap once and for all — $80 billion. 3) Argues affordability programs matter to deployment itself: predictable affordability support underpins the business case for building. 4) High-performance broadband in rural areas brings economic benefits beyond anything else that can be done for those areas. 5) Thanks Senator Klobuchar for introducing the Accessible, Affordable Internet for All Act — one of the project's anchor bills.
specific_asks: 1) Have the FCC, USDA and NTIA better coordinate standards, timelines and requirements for broadband funding awards. 2) Place greater emphasis on federal/state/Tribal coordination.
position: Industry consultant and former regulator: supports large coordinated federal investment plus predictable affordability support
verbatim_quote: "Just as the various Federal agencies such as the FCC, USDA, and NTIA should work to better coordinate on the standards, timelines, and requirements for broadband funding awards, Federal entities should place greater emphasis on federal/state/Tribal coordination." | "Predictable affordability support is actually very important to deployment, as well."

hearing: Hearings to examine recent Federal actions to expand broadband.
problem_framing: Subsidy programme design from a rural operator's experience across ReConnect, CAF and RDOF
main_arguments: 1) Midco serves more than 440,000 customers across South Dakota, North Dakota, Minnesota, Kansas and Wisconsin; most of its 400 communities have populations closer to 500 than 5,000, with farms miles apart in the Red River Valley. 2) States its identity plainly — 'what we do every day is rural broadband' — and that the remaining challenge is connecting those without any internet available, in the most rural and hard-to-reach areas. 3) Offers a concrete outcome: a $4.96 million RDOF award will reach 6,500 previously unserved locations with a wireline network capable of 5 Gbps. 4) Bases its recommendations on direct experience with ReConnect, CAF and RDOF auctions.
specific_asks: 1) Make support programs technology-neutral, encouraging the broadest participation of qualified providers and maximum flexibility. 2) Award funds through open competitive bidding. 3) Stay focused on unserved areas. 4) Improve agency coordination and enact guardrails so funds are wisely spent. 5) Continue removing barriers to deployment.
position: Regional rural cable/broadband operator: supports technology-neutral competitive bidding targeted at unserved areas
verbatim_quote: "it is critical that the programs be technology-neutral, encourage the broadest participation of qualified broadband providers, and be as flexible as possible." | "with the help of a $4.96 million award, through the FCC's RDOF program, we will reach 6,500 previously unserved locations, with a wireline broadband network capable of 5 Gbps speeds."

hearing: “LIFT America: Revitalizing our Nation’s Infrastructure and Economy”
problem_framing: Public health infrastructure as the neglected system — with distribution failures that bypass rural and vulnerable populations
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as former CDC Director (2009-2017) and New York City Health Commissioner, now leading Resolve to Save Lives. 2) Local public health departments, on the pandemic's front lines and often serving rural and vulnerable populations, lost 50,000 jobs between 2008 and 2017 to funding cuts. 3) Says plainly, acknowledging it will not make him popular in public health, that funds disbursed to state health departments are often not distributed efficiently or targeted to the areas most in need — particularly vulnerable populations and rural communities. 4) Argues embedded specialists should focus on reducing preventable illness, injury and death especially in underserved and Black, Latinx and Native American/American Indian communities.
specific_asks: 1) Require health defense operations programs to submit a bypass professional judgment budget to Congress annually, giving Congress an unvarnished view of what is needed. 2) Fund rapid response funds, health worker protection, and data/laboratory/disease monitoring systems. 3) Sustain public health infrastructure at the level actually required.
position: Public health leadership: supports sustained infrastructure funding with better targeting to underserved and rural populations
verbatim_quote: "Our local public health departments, those on the front lines of this pandemic, often providing support for rural and vulnerable populations, lost 50,000 jobs between 2008 and 2017 due to funding cuts." | "all too often, funds disbursed to state health departments are not distributed efficiently and effectively, and not sufficiently targeted to the areas most in need of assistance, particularly vulnerable populations, and rural communities."

hearing: “LIFT America: Revitalizing our Nation’s Infrastructure and Economy”
problem_framing: Grid modernisation as multi-objective infrastructure policy, with social equity named as one of the objectives
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as former Energy Secretary, framing the Texas grid disaster as a wake-up call for the LIFT America Act's energy infrastructure provisions. 2) Draws on the Quadrennial Energy Review: its installment made 63 recommendations on a smarter cleaner grid, workforce training, emissions from gas systems, waterborne transport and siting/permitting; 29 were fully implemented by the end of his tenure with 21 more underway. 3) Argues grid modernisation must meet multiple objectives simultaneously: clean reliable service to growing demand, promoting social equity and inclusion, resilience against climate and cyber threats, integrating distributed clean electricity, and supporting broad connectivity across the system. 4) Recommends flexible financing and capacity building at federal, state and local levels, while maximising consumer equity.
specific_asks: 1) Provide flexible financing for a clean, modernised grid. 2) Prepare the grid for climate and cyber risks. 3) Build federal, state and local regulatory capacity. 4) Maximise consumer equity and economic value of the system.
position: Former federal energy official: supports the LIFT America Act's grid modernisation with equity and resilience objectives
verbatim_quote: "electric grid modernization must meet multiple objectives: providing clean, reliable service to growing demand; promoting social equity and inclusion; ensuring resilient performance in the face of a changing climate and increasing cyber threats; integrating distributed sources of clean electricity; and supporting broad connectivity throughout the system"

hearing: “LIFT America: Revitalizing our Nation’s Infrastructure and Economy”
problem_framing: Broadband subsidy as a targeting problem — the unserved population is shrinking and money must not go where private capital already serves
main_arguments: 1) Testifies on the communications portions of H.R. 1848, the LIFT America Act, as a former FCC Commissioner now consulting and at the Hudson Institute. 2) Argues the number of unserved Americans continues to shrink precipitously, though the exact count is uncertain because of mapping problems. 3) Identifies two proven ways to extend broadband to the unserved, the first being very targeted, well thought-out subsidy programs that focus directly on unserved Americans and exclude areas the private sector already serves. 4) Cites his own record on Connect America Fund reform, standalone broadband for rate-of-return providers, the Alternative Connect America Cost Model, and reverse auctions promoting efficiency.
specific_asks: Design broadband subsidy narrowly — target unserved Americans directly and exclude areas already served by the private sector
position: Former regulator: supports narrowly targeted deployment subsidy, sceptical of broader programs

hearing: “5G and Beyond: Exploring the Next Wireless Frontier”
problem_framing: Spectrum supply as the precondition for everything 5G delivers — with digital inclusion now listed first among those benefits
main_arguments: 1) Every benefit being experienced with 5G — expanding digital inclusion, economic growth, job creation, smart cities, improvements in public safety, health care and the environment — is predicated on spectrum availability, with digital inclusion named first. 2) America is playing catch-up but can maintain global leadership with the right policies. 3) Attacks the shared-access model on cost and speed: CBRS requires five times as many cell sites for suburban coverage and at least seven times as many in rural areas, raising costs and slowing build-out, and its sharing regime took about eight years from proposal to auction against three for C-band and two for 3.45 GHz. 4) Demand projections — a 24-fold increase in 5G subscriptions by 2026 and over 500 percent growth in wireless data — require several hundred megahertz per provider.
specific_asks: 1) Expeditiously extend the FCC's auction authority. 2) Support the Spectrum Innovation Act to bring critical mid-band spectrum to auction. 3) Identify and set clear deadlines for future low-, mid- and high-band access at the same time. 4) Consider the 1.3-1.35 GHz, 1.124-1.164 GHz and 1.78-1.83 GHz bands, and set a timetable for the 26, 42 and 50 GHz high bands.
position: Wireless industry association: supports exclusive licensed spectrum and auction authority, critical of the CBRS sharing model
verbatim_quote: "CBRS requires five times as many cell sites for coverage in suburban areas, and at least seven times as many in rural areas—significantly increasing costs, the time to deploy, and slowing 5G network buildout." | "Every benefit that we are experiencing with 5G in the U.S.—expanding digital inclusion, economic growth, job creation, smart cities, and improvements in public safety, health care, and our environment—is predicated on the availability of spectrum."

main_arguments: 1) Over two years Americans experienced the power of an affordable high-speed connection for schooling, remote work and telehealth, which galvanised support for investing the resources needed to end the divide that still persists. 2) Lists the agency's own record: increasing choice and competition, standing up the largest set of affordability programs in FCC history, expanding telehealth access and freeing spectrum. 3) On deployment cost, argues the FCC's cost-sharing rules for pole replacements should not inhibit internet builds, particularly in unserved areas. 4) Raises a funding-coordination gap: the IIJA's prioritisation scheme does not apply to Treasury's ARPA broadband funds. 5) Adds a distinct Section 230 agenda about platform censorship.

verbatim_quote: "While that IIJA provision does not apply to Treasury's ARPA funds, Congress should consider passing a new law that requires ARPA expenditures to track the IIJA's prioritization scheme." | "I argued that the FCC should make sure that our cost sharing rules for pole replacements are not inhibiting Internet builds, particularly in unserved areas."

verbatim_quote: "And like so many other aspects of the pandemic, the lack of access to and adoption of home broadband has amplified and reinforced existing inequities in our society." | "Congress and President Biden have made a $14.2 billion investment in affordability that converted the Emergency Broadband Benefit from a pandemic-focused effort into a long-term part of the FCC's work."
