hearing: An oversight hearing to examine the National Telecommunications and Information Administration.
problem_framing: The agency's own framing at the moment BEAD begins — closing the digital divide as NTIA's declared top priority
main_arguments: 1) Speaks as Assistant Secretary for Communications and Information at what he calls a historic moment for NTIA, having been confirmed in January. 2) By law NTIA advises the President on telecommunications and information policy; its programs expand broadband access and adoption, promote spectrum use by all users, and keep the internet an engine of innovation and growth — access and adoption named together. 3) States the top priority without qualification: closing the digital divide, noting the country has been talking about it for over 20 years. 4) Identifies the resource: the law provided $65 billion to help deliver affordable, reliable, high-speed internet to every American.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt — an oversight statement reporting agency priorities and IIJA implementation progress
position: Federal agency administering BEAD: frames closing the divide as NTIA's top priority under the $65 billion IIJA allocation
verbatim_quote: "Our top priority is closing the digital divide. We have been talking about the digital divide in this country for over 20 years." | "The law provided, as you know, $65 billion to help deliver affordable, reliable, high speed Internet to every American."

hearing: Hearings to examine the future of spectrum.
problem_framing: Spectrum reallocation as an interagency-process audit — whether FCC and NTIA can resolve disputes on agreed technical findings
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as GAO's Director of Physical Infrastructure as the Committee examines federal spectrum management and reauthorisation of the FCC's auction authority. 2) Explains the split responsibility: the FCC regulates commercial and non-federal use, NTIA manages federal use. 3) Notes the reauthorisation legislation seeks to make 200 megahertz currently used by federal agencies available for 5G, and that NTIA's key role is examining band suitability for reallocation. 4) Reports that GAO made recommendations to both agencies, that they agreed to work collaboratively, and that the MOU released that day should create a framework for resolving reallocation disagreements based on agreed technical findings. 5) Documents the follow-through: the FCC affirmed implementation in January 2022 and NTIA indicated it was working on the June 2021 recommendations in February 2022.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a new request — the testimony reports on implementation of GAO's existing recommendations to the FCC and NTIA
position: Federal audit agency: assesses interagency spectrum coordination; supports resolving reallocation disputes on agreed technical findings
verbatim_quote: "The agencies have agreed to work collaboratively and have begun to implement our recommendations, as evidenced by the MOU released today, which we believe will help create a framework where disagreements regarding the reallocation of spectrum can be resolved based on agreed upon technical findings."

hearing: Hearings to examine the future of spectrum.
problem_framing: Spectrum policy anchored in statutory public interest objectives — with auction revenue proposed as a funding source for digital inclusion
main_arguments: 1) Offers four guideposts for national spectrum strategy aimed at innovation and quality access for all. 2) The first centres the public interest objectives Congress already set: the Telecommunications Act directed the FCC to design auctions with safeguards promoting competition and economic opportunity, preventing excessive consolidation and creating opportunities for small businesses, especially minority and women-owned. 3) Points to results for Tribes: the FCC has distributed 335 licences covering 350 Tribes in over 30 states through the rural Tribal window. 4) Argues the CBRS takeaway is that openness to the full suite of access regimes lets policymakers use large swaths of spectrum efficiently. 5) States that digital equity programs knock down barriers to adoption and help communities make greater use of connectivity.
specific_asks: 1) Require the FCC to create a Tribal priority window before any future commercial auction. 2) Order the FCC and NTIA to explore extending CBRS-style sharing for Native Americans on Tribal lands. 3) Support the Airways for Equity Initiative, setting aside auction revenues to fund digital inclusion, next-generation 911 and rip-and-replace. 4) Grant a longer reauthorisation that does not primarily mandate the next auction, signalling future auctions without dictating their timeline.
position: Public-interest advocacy: supports Tribal spectrum access, shared spectrum and earmarking auction revenue for digital inclusion
verbatim_quote: "Public Knowledge supports the Airways for Equity Initiative, which proposes setting aside spectrum auction revenues to fund digital inclusion efforts, completing next gen 911, finishing the work of rip and replace" | "Congress should require that prior to any future commercial auction of spectrum, the FCC create a similar window for Tribes to apply."

hearing: Hearings to examine the future of spectrum.
problem_framing: Spectrum as a scarce commonly-owned resource whose value is realised only through use — reallocation always creates losers
main_arguments: 1) Radio spectrum is a scarce natural resource owned by all and used by all, and value is created only through using it — smartphones on licensed spectrum, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on unlicensed, and public missions on government assignments. 2) All these uses compete for a fixed pool managed by the FCC and NTIA, whose goal is extracting the most from it. 3) States the political economy plainly: all spectrum has incumbent users, so somebody loses whenever spectrum is reallocated, and the easier reallocations have already been done. 4) Frames spectrum policy as informing everything from global competitiveness to making broadband accessible and affordable, arguing that if closing the divide is serious, good spectrum policy must be a top priority.
specific_asks: When extending auction authority, ensure the Commission can immediately begin planning its future slate of auctions and start the complex technical evaluations and negotiations with incumbent users
position: Economic consultant: supports extending auction authority with immediate forward planning; frames spectrum policy as central to closing the divide
verbatim_quote: "Their challenge is that all spectrum has incumbent users. That is, somebody loses when spectrum is reallocated. Over time, the easier reallocations have been done" | "If we are serious about closing the digital divide, developing good policy here must be a top priority."

hearing: Hearings to examine the future of spectrum.
problem_framing: Licensed mid-band spectrum as the precondition for 5G home broadband, presented as the cost-effective way to extend federal broadband dollars
main_arguments: 1) Reports 5G deploying almost twice as fast as 4G, with $30 billion a year invested in infrastructure — 2019's promise now delivered. 2) Makes the central claim linking spectrum to the divide: the fastest growing home broadband company is a wireless provider, and 5G home will be key to closing the digital divide. 3) Argues 5G home broadband is a scalable, cost-effective solution that extends the reach of the federal dollars Congress appropriated for unserved and underserved locations. 4) Repeats the list in which digital inclusion now comes first among 5G's benefits, all predicated on spectrum availability. 5) Renews the attack on CBRS, which requires five times as many cell sites for coverage.
specific_asks: 1) Re-up the FCC's auction authority, supporting the House's bipartisan 18-month extension. 2) Replenish the spectrum pipeline, passing the Spectrum Innovation Act to open the lower 3 GHz band. 3) Revitalise interagency coordination. 4) Add low-band and high-band allocations and investigate the 7-15 GHz range for future commercial access.
position: Wireless industry association: supports licensed mid-band expansion, framing fixed wireless as a BEAD-stretching divide solution
verbatim_quote: "The fastest growing home broadband company is a wireless provider and 5G home will be key in closing the digital divide." | "5G home broadband is a scalable, cost-effective solution that can extend the reach of these Federal dollars and close the digital divide."

hearing: Hearings to examine solutions to meet America's broadband needs.
problem_framing: Digital equity as community capacity built during the pandemic — the people doing adoption work named as the constituency
main_arguments: 1) NDIA advances digital equity by supporting community programs and equipping policymakers to act. 2) States the historical claim precisely: digital inequities are not new, but the pandemic made them painfully clear, and that clarity calls for action. 3) Credits the field rather than the state: communities scaled up existing digital inclusion programs, created new ones and took risks on innovative solutions — she calls them the country's digital equity heroes. 4) Attributes the progress to Congress's swift pandemic actions, positioning the digital equity community as a constituency with standing before the Committee. 5) Raises a guardrail against duplicative spending across federal programs.
specific_asks: 1) Confirm the pending nomination before the holiday recess. 2) Require a certification process by which agencies certify that their use of federal funds would not deploy in areas where federal funds are already being spent.
position: Digital inclusion advocacy: supports sustained federal funding for community adoption programs plus anti-duplication guardrails
verbatim_quote: "Digital inequities are not new, but the pandemic made them painfully clear." | "Communities came together, scaled up existing digital inclusion programs, set up new programs, took risks on innovative solutions. They are our country's digital equity heroes."

hearing: Hearings to examine solutions to meet America's broadband needs.
problem_framing: BEAD as a once-in-a-generation chance to finish a build the market could not justify — cost, not willingness, framed as the barrier
main_arguments: 1) NCTA members invested hundreds of billions over 20 years to reach 90 percent of households, but the work is undone. 2) States the market-limit argument directly: many members would like to serve rural and unserved areas but cannot, because they are cost-prohibitive without public support. 3) Frames the scale as unprecedented — ten times the money allocated in the earlier 2009-era program — addressing the core concern in unserved areas, and the first meaningful opportunity to genuinely close the divide. 4) Notes, as a point he considers under-discussed, that Congress took a fresh approach to adoption and affordability, not only deployment. 5) Identifies pole access as the practical bottleneck.
specific_asks: Require all utility pole owners to provide timely and non-discriminatory access to poles, ducts, conduits and rights-of-way at non-discriminatory rates
position: Cable industry association: supports BEAD-scale public funding and pole access reform as the deployment bottleneck
verbatim_quote: "Many of our members would love to serve rural and unserved parts of the country but are unable to do so because they are cost prohibitive without public support." | "This scale of resources provides the first meaningful opportunity to genuinely close the digital divide"

hearing: Hearings to examine solutions to meet America's broadband needs.
problem_framing: Universal connectivity framed by the industry association itself as a matter of digital equity
main_arguments: 1) USTelecom represents providers from the largest publicly traded investors to local cooperatives with roots going back over a century. 2) States that the pandemic laid bare the unacceptable cost of being left on the wrong side of the digital divide. 3) Uses the equity vocabulary in its own voice: universal connectivity is a matter of digital equity, and the collective work is not done. 4) Cautions against oversimplifying what achieving affordable, reliable, high-speed internet for all requires, offering providers as committed partners. 5) Supports making low-income connectivity support permanent rather than temporary.
specific_asks: 1) Pass S. 5021, the Broadband Grant Tax Treatment Act, so grant resources stay in the communities they serve rather than being taxed back. 2) Pass the FAIR Contributions Act. 3) Make the Affordable Connectivity Program permanent.
position: Broadband industry association: supports permanent ACP, grant tax relief and broadening the universal service contribution base
verbatim_quote: "Universal connectivity is a matter of digital equity, and our collective work is not yet done." | "Congress should make permanent this commitment to connecting low-income households."

hearing: Hearings to examine solutions to meet America's broadband needs.
problem_framing: Tribal self-provision as the answer where no provider ever came — and the BEAD map challenge deadline as the immediate threat
main_arguments: 1) Speaks as a Hopi tribal member and Chief Technology Director of the Santa Fe Indian School, chairing the Connect New Mexico Council, in one of the least connected states because of rugged terrain and sparse density. 2) Gives the baseline: wireline ISP offerings in her community have not changed in 20 years — there are none — and until she completed the first fibre network in 2018 the entire tribal government and public library shared a 3.0 Mbps bonded T1. 3) During COVID she had to connect 700 students sent home to 23 rural tribal communities among the least connected lands in the country. 4) States the sovereignty argument: the Tribal Broadband Connectivity Program springboards tribal efforts to connect unserved homes and anchor institutions, and experience proves 'we can be our own solution to the digital divide'. 5) Some tribal entities now participate in the ACP as service providers.
specific_asks: Ask NTIA to extend the January 13, 2023 deadline for challenging locations missing from the FCC's preliminary broadband map, so they can be counted
position: Tribal education and state broadband council: supports tribal-owned networks and a longer BEAD map challenge window
verbatim_quote: "TBCP springboards tribal efforts to connect unserved homes and anchor institutions, and our experience has proven that we can be our own solution to the digital divide." | "We ask NTIA to extend the January 13, 2023, deadline to have more time to challenge the missing location to the FCC's preliminary broadband map."

hearing: Launching into the State of the Satellite Marketplace
problem_framing: Satellite positioned as the most viable technology for bridging the rural divide — technology-inclusive policy as the ask
main_arguments: 1) SIA represents satellite operators, service providers, manufacturers, launch providers and ground equipment suppliers; satellites are described as the backbone of modern society for communications, navigation and remote sensing. 2) Claims the industry already provides FCC-defined broadband service globally and is positioned to bring the furthest corners of America into the 21st century. 3) Frames satellite as the most viable technology capable of bridging the rural divide while also serving as backbone for 5G, IoT and AI. 4) Grounds it in agriculture: satellite broadband enables remote farms with livestock sensors, soil monitors and autonomous equipment far beyond where terrestrial networks reach or make economic sense.
specific_asks: Adopt technology-inclusive policies that allow innovative solutions across domains to address connectivity needs (i.e., do not exclude satellite from federal broadband programs)
position: Satellite industry association: supports technology-neutral eligibility so satellite qualifies for federal broadband funding
verbatim_quote: "The satellite industry provides FCC-defined broadband service today across the globe and is prepared to bring the furthest corners of America into the 21st Century by serving as the most viable technology capable of bridging the digital divide in rural areas"

hearing: Launching into the State of the Satellite Marketplace
problem_framing: Satellite eligibility in BEAD as the concrete stake — cost-effectiveness and timeliness against fibre's build time
main_arguments: 1) Testifies for EchoStar, founded 1980, on satellite technology's role for US and global users. 2) States that satellite broadband service is critical to a cost-effective and timely solution to the divide, with the Hughes broadband business focused on underserved communities. 3) Offers the equity claim in concrete terms: HughesNet and competing services mean a student in rural Ohio can access the same information as a student in urban Cleveland in real time. 4) Notes satellite operators already participate in the Connect America Fund and RDOF, and turns explicitly to BEAD at NTIA. 5) On spectrum, resists sharing obligations, arguing the FCC should not adopt untested and unproven sharing requirements for the relevant bands.
specific_asks: 1) In oversight of BEAD and related programs, ensure they enable the use of satellite broadband technology. 2) Ensure adequate FCC funding to handle increased satellite licensing activity. 3) Do not adopt untested sharing requirements for satellite bands.
position: Satellite operator: supports satellite eligibility in BEAD and opposes new spectrum sharing mandates
verbatim_quote: "we urge this Subcommittee in your oversight of BEAD and related or future programs to ensure that they enable the use of satellite broadband technology." | "Satellite broadband service is critical if we are to have a cost-effective and timely solution to solving the digital divide."

hearing: Launching into the State of the Satellite Marketplace
problem_framing: Low Earth orbit constellations as a means of delivering affordable service specifically to unserved and underserved communities
main_arguments: 1) Project Kuiper is a constellation of 3,236 satellites in low Earth orbit, whose stated mission is delivering fast, affordable broadband to unserved and underserved communities in the US and worldwide. 2) The scale-and-innovation argument: the company judged it could deliver an affordable, high-speed solution to tens of millions of customers in those communities. 3) Technically, the satellites are designed for speeds, latency and reliability on par with terrestrial networks, deliverable in rural and remote areas almost anywhere. 4) Cites breakthroughs in customer terminals that are small, high-performing and affordable — addressing the historic cost barrier of satellite equipment.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a discrete legislative request — the testimony presents the constellation's capability and mission
position: Satellite operator (new entrant): positions LEO service as an affordable option for unserved and underserved communities
verbatim_quote: "Our mission is to deliver fast, affordable broadband to unserved and underserved communities in the United States and around the world." | "Our satellites are designed to deliver broadband service with speeds, latency, and reliability on par with terrestrial networks and to provide this connectivity in rural and remote areas almost anywhere in the world."

organization: Center for Strategic and International Studies
hearing: Launching into the State of the Satellite Marketplace
problem_framing: Space competition and national security, with satellite broadband constellations presented as a divide-bridging market opportunity
main_arguments: 1) Testifies on space technology trends, foreign competition and US leadership, noting CSIS takes no policy positions so the views are her own. 2) Frames space-based broadband constellations as a compelling solution for bridging the divide, citing nearly 40 percent of the world's population unconnected. 3) For the US specifically, cites 28 percent of rural households — roughly 4.8 million Americans — as unconnected, drawing on Pew and USDA sources. 4) Argues the market potential is high as consumers and businesses demand more bandwidth, speed and quality — the divide framed as addressable demand rather than only as a policy obligation.
specific_asks: FCC regulatory reform, among a set of recommendations aimed at maintaining US leadership in space and the competitive position of US space companies
position: Think tank (aerospace security): supports regulatory reform to sustain US space competitiveness, citing divide-bridging as a market case
verbatim_quote: "These space -based broadband internet constellations offer a compelling solution for bridging the digital divide, where nearly 40 percent of the world's population remain unconnected." | "In the United States alone, 28 percent of rural households (roughly 4.8 million Americans) remain unconnected."

hearing: Launching into the State of the Satellite Marketplace
problem_framing: Satellite licensing speed as a competitiveness question, with 'digital poverty' framed around the device people already own
main_arguments: 1) Answering questions for the record as co-founder and COO of Lynk Global on international licensing practice. 2) Argues the US is a world leader in setting the standard for responsible licensing, but that the process once matched an industry made up of 'Old Space' companies and must adapt to the new paradigm. 3) Countries seeking to maintain space leadership must offer affordable, responsible and fast licensing. 4) Introduces a distinct framing of the access problem: digital poverty is growing, and affordable connectivity that works with the device a person already has or can afford is key to closing the gap — connectivity built around existing handsets rather than new terminals. 5) Raises regulatory forum shopping as a risk to be closed off.
specific_asks: 1) Ensure an affordable, timely and transparent US regulatory process to support American innovation. 2) Have the FCC shut down forum shopping by denying US market access to bad-actor satellite firms and encouraging allied regulators and the ITU to do the same.
position: Satellite new entrant: supports faster, cheaper licensing and regulatory coordination against forum shopping
verbatim_quote: "Digital poverty is growing and affordable connectivity that supports the device a person has or c an afford is key to closing the gap." | "The Federal Communications Commission should play an important role in shutting down forum shopping by preventing market access in the United States to bad actor satellite firms"

hearing: Liftoff: Unleashing Innovation in Satellite Communications Technologies
problem_framing: NTIA's satellite and international spectrum work, presented from the office that manages federal spectrum
main_arguments: 1) Testifies on behalf of Assistant Secretary Alan Davidson as Chief of the International Spectrum Policy Division in NTIA's Office of Spectrum Management, a role held for eight years. 2) Frames the testimony around NTIA's work on satellite issues and Department of Commerce space activity. 3) Positions NTIA's spectrum management function as the federal counterpart to the FCC's commercial licensing in satellite policy.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt — an agency statement describing NTIA's satellite and international spectrum work rather than requesting legislation
position: Federal agency: describes NTIA's role in satellite and international spectrum policy; no distinct position captured in the excerpt
verbatim_quote: "I serve as the Chief of the International Spectrum Policy Division in NTIA's Office of Spectrum Management (OSM) and have been in that role for the past eight years."

hearing: Liftoff: Unleashing Innovation in Satellite Communications Technologies
problem_framing: Licensing timelines as a bottleneck on connecting unserved Americans — regulatory delay framed as the reason constellations are built before approval
main_arguments: 1) Answering questions for the record on the difference between launch and satellite approval processes: the FAA licenses commercial launches and re-entries to protect the uninvolved public, while the FCC licenses the spectrum used to communicate with rockets and spacecraft. 2) Launch providers also work with federal ranges within NASA and the US Space Force. 3) Makes the operative claim about timing: extreme demand to connect unserved Americans quickly, combined with lengthy regulatory reviews, drives US licensees to begin building complex constellations years before their licence is granted — the delay is absorbed as private risk. 4) Raises regulatory arbitrage, with foreign-licensed systems able to evade US regulation.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a discrete request — the answers argue for faster US licensing and for closing the gap that lets foreign-licensed systems evade US rules
position: Satellite operator: seeks faster licensing and action against foreign-licensed systems evading US regulation
verbatim_quote: "The extreme demand to connect unserved Americans quickly, coupled with a lengthy timeline for regulatory reviews, ... drive U.S. licensees to begin work on these complex satellite constellations years before the license is granted."

hearing: Liftoff: Unleashing Innovation in Satellite Communications Technologies
problem_framing: Legacy satellite operator framing — emergency access and rural agriculture as the connectivity gaps satellite fills
main_arguments: 1) Traces the company's origin to President Kennedy signing the Communications Satellite Act in 1962, through to satellite life-extension projects in 2020, describing its DNA as collaboration plus technological innovation. 2) Presents itself as a long-standing steward of the space ecosystem wanting to preserve the space environment for future generations. 3) Argues everyone deserves access to emergency services regardless of where they live, and supports legislation moving toward that goal. 4) Supports the Precision Agriculture Connectivity Act's goal of connecting hard-to-reach rural areas, noting much US agricultural production occurs in very rural places without terrestrial service.
specific_asks: Support the pending emergency-services legislation and the goal of the Precision Agriculture Connectivity Act to provide connectivity to hard-to-reach rural areas
position: Incumbent satellite operator: supports satellite's role in emergency access and rural agricultural connectivity
verbatim_quote: "Everyone deserves to have access to emergency services no matter where they live, and this legislation moves us closer to this goal." | "Much of the agricultural production in the U.S. takes place in very rural areas, some of which do not have access to terrestrial service."

hearing: Liftoff: Unleashing Innovation in Satellite Communications Technologies
problem_framing: International spectrum negotiation as the frame — connectivity and broadband access as the ITU mission the agency supports
main_arguments: 1) Answering the Chair's question on Administration priorities at the World Radiocommunication Conference, states FCC support for the ITU's core mission of promoting connectivity and broadband access and fostering a flexible international regulatory framework. 2) Describes four years of staff engagement in the ITU preparatory study cycle for WRC-23, fostering opportunities for new satellite and terrestrial operations and participating in sharing studies to ensure compatibility across spectrum access technologies. 3) Domestically, the agency collaborates with the public and private sectors to align WRC priorities with its own initiatives, and with federal partners so new band access accounts for US interests in science and safety.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt — answers for the record describing the agency's WRC preparation and priorities
position: Federal regulator: supports international spectrum coordination advancing connectivity and compatibility across technologies
verbatim_quote: "the FCC is supportive of the ITU's core mission of promoting connectivity, broadband access, and fostering a flexible international regulatory framework for an evolving telecommunications ecosystem."

hearing: Liftoff: Unleashing Innovation in Satellite Communications Technologies
problem_framing: Orbital debris and space sustainability as a coordination problem, with Earth-observation data as the policy payoff
main_arguments: 1) Answering questions for the record, argues that protecting the orbital operating environment is a global problem requiring global participation, and an opportunity for US leadership to work with industry on standard practices for space situational awareness data, deconfliction between operators and debris reduction. 2) Notes US agencies currently work independently on orbital debris and sustainability, creating an opening to collaborate on policy and avoid conflicting or duplicative regulation, then lead peers toward adopting US standards. 3) Shifts to terrestrial benefit: satellite data supports new research in agricultural practices, air and water quality and forest health, which targeted congressional R&D investment could accelerate.
specific_asks: 1) Coordinate across US agencies on orbital debris and space sustainability policy to avoid duplicative regulation and lead global adoption of US standards. 2) Make targeted R&D investments accelerating integration of space-based technology and data into decision making, including in agriculture.
position: Earth-observation satellite company: supports coordinated debris regulation and federal R&D investment in space data applications
verbatim_quote: "there is an opportunity to closely collaborate on policy developments to avoid conflicting or duplicative regulation and then lead among their global peers to encourage adoption of U.S. standard practices."

hearing: Liftoff: Unleashing Innovation in Satellite Communications Technologies
problem_framing: Direct answer to whether satellite licensing caused the digital divide — the witness says no, but flags spectrum scarcity and processing-round strain
main_arguments: 1) Asked directly whether FCC and NTIA regulatory barriers contributed to the digital divide by making satellite systems hard to license, answers that the FCC's licensing system has not delayed satellite connectivity in remote parts of the country nor actively contributed to the divide — an explicit refusal of the premise. 2) Qualifies it: the system, together with a lack of available spectrum for satellite operations in UHF and S-band, has led operators to consider filing offshore through overseas administrations. 3) Explains the structural strain: the FCC inherited a processing-round approach that struggles with today's volume and complexity — since 2016 more than twenty entities have filed for over 70,000 satellites for NGSO FSS spectrum alone.
specific_asks: Not stated in excerpt as a discrete request — the answer identifies spectrum scarcity and the processing-round approach as the issues to address
position: Academic engineer: rejects the claim that satellite licensing caused the divide, while identifying spectrum scarcity and process strain
verbatim_quote: NOTE: this witness's PDF extracted without spaces between words; quote transcribed exactly as stored and must be checked against the original — "TheFCC'slicensingsystemhasnot delayedsatelliteconnectivityinremotepartsof thecountry,nor hasit activelycontributedtothecurrent digital divide."

hearing: Defending America’s Wireless Leadership
problem_framing: Full-power licensed access as the requirement for rural 5G — shared low-power frameworks framed as raising rural cost
main_arguments: 1) Thanks the Subcommittee for bipartisan work on auction authority and repurposing spectrum for 5G, arguing US leadership in licensed and unlicensed wireless rests on that focus. 2) Frames the rural stake: as Congress considers future commercial access it must keep in view that 5G needs to reach rural and exurban communities with the security and reliability applications require. 3) Renews the technical attack on shared spectrum: the complex sharing system has not worked as envisioned, and its low-power design means operators must build as many as seven times more towers in rural areas to reach the same community, raising the cost of serving rural Americans. 4) Argues federal spectrum governance needs a single authoritative voice.
specific_asks: 1) Seek solutions providing full power commercial access without risk of federal preemption over commercial use. 2) Elevate the NTIA Administrator to Under Secretary level within the Department of Commerce so NTIA speaks for the Executive Branch with one voice.
position: Wireless industry association: supports full-power exclusive licensing and stronger NTIA authority, opposed to low-power sharing regimes
verbatim_quote: "That complex sharing system has not yet worked as envisioned and its low power design means 10 operators need to build as many as seven times more towers in rural areas to reach the same community, increasing the cost to serving rural Americans." | "Congress can send all stakeholders a clear signal about NTIA's critical role by elevating the Administrator's position to the Under Secretary level within the Department of Commerce."

hearing: Defending America’s Wireless Leadership
problem_framing: Spectrum availability as a strategic question, answered on the federal-commercial balance between Commerce and Defense
main_arguments: 1) Answering a question for the record about whether he supports the Commerce and Defense Departments' joint position on auction authority and spectrum availability, as set out in their 5 March 2023 letter. 2) Restates the position given in oral testimony: US leadership in wireless communications is a strategic matter. 3) Situates the answer in the agreed interagency process for studying the impact of opening 3 GHz spectrum to commercial use on existing federal missions.
specific_asks: Not stated in the captured excerpt — the response addresses the Commerce/Defense position on auction authority without a distinct legislative request being captured
position: Think tank: treats wireless leadership as strategic; full position on the Commerce/Defense letter not captured in the excerpt
verbatim_quote: "As I testified to the subcommittee on March 10, 2023, I believe that U.S. leadership in wireless communications is a strate[gic]"

hearing: Defending America’s Wireless Leadership
problem_framing: Budget scoring rules as a hidden thumb on the scale — the auction-revenue frame biasing policy against shared and unlicensed spectrum
main_arguments: 1) NCTA represents cable operators serving roughly 90 percent of cable television households; over the past 10 years cable companies invested more than $172 billion in fibre-rich deployment and upgrades, including in low-income, rural and remote areas. 2) Argues spectrum access is essential to cable's ability to compete and to any small, rural or non-traditional wireless provider developing new connectivity services. 3) Notes spectrum's growing importance for private networks used in industrial automation, AI and predictive maintenance. 4) Identifies the structural bias: budget scoring rules over-index the value of auction receipts relative to the economic value and competition created by shared-licensed and unlicensed frameworks.
specific_asks: Remove the implicit bias toward exclusive auctions embedded in budget scoring rules, which over-values auction receipts against the economic value and competition created by shared-licensed and unlicensed spectrum
position: Cable industry association: supports shared and unlicensed spectrum access, against exclusive-auction bias in budget scoring
verbatim_quote: "we urge Congress to remove the implicit bias toward exclusive auctions that is reflected in budget scoring rules that over-indexes the value of auction receipts over the economic value and competition created by spectrum that is made available through the auctioned shared-licensed framework as well by unlicensed use."

hearing: Defending America’s Wireless Leadership
problem_framing: Divide as twin problems of availability and affordability requiring equity of service across rural, inner-city and suburban America
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as an electrical engineering professor and SpectrumX policy outreach director with joint appointments at Chicago and Argonne. 2) States the framing explicitly: bridging the divide requires attention to both availability and affordability, to ensure equity of services between rural, inner-city urban and suburban residents — inner-city named alongside rural. 3) Differentiates the problem geographically: in most rural areas the issue is availability of fixed and mobile broadband. 4) Describes BEAD as overseeing fibre deployments bringing 100/20 Mbps to all 'serviceable' locations identified in the FCC's National Broadband Map. 5) Suggests alternate architectures such as satellite backhaul with local distribution over shared spectrum in a private network. 6) Links spectrum policy to industrial policy through chip supply.
specific_asks: 1) Ensure synergies that leverage the CHIPS and Science Act to encourage innovation in wireless chips and semiconductor systems. 2) Ensure that innovations encouraged by forward-looking spectrum policy are not held back by limited access to chipsets.
position: Academic engineer: supports combining availability and affordability measures, alternate architectures and CHIPS-linked wireless innovation
verbatim_quote: "Bridging the digital divide will require attention to both availability and affordability of broadband to ensure that there is equity of services available between rural, inner-city urban and suburban residents across America." | "NTIA's Broadband, Equity, Access and Deployment (BEAD) program will oversee fiber deployments that will bring true broadband (defined as a minimum of 100 Mbps downlink and 20 Mbps uplink, or 100/20) to all “serviceable” locations as identified in FCC's National Broadband Map."

main_arguments: 1) Testifies as a Stanford health policy professor and NBER research associate, stating he was specifically targeted for censorship by federal government officials because of his views on COVID-19 restrictions. 2) In October 2020 he and colleagues at Harvard and Oxford published the Great Barrington Declaration, calling for an end to economic lockdowns and school shutdowns. 3) The declaration's substantive claim was distributive: those restrictions disproportionately harm the young and economically disadvantaged while conferring limited benefits. 4) Grounds the argument in stratified vulnerability to COVID-19 mortality.

hearing: Preserving Free Speech and Reining in Big Tech Censorship

main_arguments: 1) WIA represents the companies that build, design, own and manage mobile and fixed wireless infrastructure. 2) Argues the country has never been closer to nationwide connectivity — broadband available from dense urban cores to the last rural acre — and that broadband has never been more available, affordable, accessible and competitive, a win worth acknowledging even with work remaining. 3) Cites demand growth: monthly data usage expected to rise nearly 30 percent over five years to over 85 exabytes per month. 4) Reads BEAD's design as an endorsement: in solving the divide, Congress recognised the value of fixed wireless by making the program technology neutral. 5) Identifies FAA review backlog as a resource problem.

hearing: Breaking Barriers: Streamlining Permitting to Expedite Broadband Deployment

main_arguments: 1) Testifies as an FCC Commissioner from 2013 to 2020 and former House and Senate staffer, now consulting. 2) Argues that despite changing definitions of speed and capacity over time, the charge has stayed constant: bring private sector broadband to every unserved household. 3) Notes NTIA Administrator Davidson had recently spoken publicly on the necessity of permitting reform and pole attachments to make BEAD grants effective — an alignment between the agency and the witness. 4) Raises the affordability side explicitly: as access expands through these programs, overall affordability still needs addressing, and the Affordable Connectivity Program is likely to exhaust its resources mid-next year. 5) Argues Congress can affirm the Commission's authority and empower other agencies or courts to remove barriers.
specific_asks: 1) Enact the bills before the Subcommittee, affirming the FCC's authority and granting other agencies or courts authority to remove permitting barriers. 2) Make additional funding for the Affordable Connectivity Program a priority before it exhausts its resources.
position: Former regulator: supports permitting and pole attachment reform plus continued ACP funding
verbatim_quote: "I have made the case that championing added funding for the Affordable Connectivity Program (ACP), which is likely to exhaust resources mid-next year, should be a priority by Subcommittee Members" | "NTIA Administrator Alan Davidson recently spoke publicly about the necessity of permitting reform, and its compatriot pole attachments, to effectuate his agency's broadband funding grants"

hearing: Oversight of the Federal Communications Commission
problem_framing: Broadband as essential for full participation in modern life, with the ACP and the National Broadband Map as the agency's two instruments
main_arguments: 1) Reiterates that the pandemic proved broadband access is essential for full participation in modern life, and that there is no substitute for meeting people where they live and work. 2) Reports the ACP as the largest broadband affordability program in the nation's history, now helping more than 18 million households pay for service. 3) Describes the National Broadband Map as the most accurate ever created and as an instrument that will help close the divide — data as policy infrastructure. 4) Notes a mechanism letting survivors receive emergency communications support from Lifeline or the ACP for up to six months, extending affordability policy to domestic violence survivors.

hearing: Oversight of the Federal Communications Commission
problem_framing: Auction authority and agency process as the agenda, with the ACP questioned on whether it buys adoption or subsidises existing purchases
main_arguments: 1) Reports the agency as productive and focused on efficient spectrum use, network security and preserving Earth orbit. 2) Argues renewal of auction authority is crucial to US wireless leadership, given the private sector's unquenchable thirst for spectrum. 3) Defends the auction model on institutional grounds: allocating spectrum by auction forces proposed uses to tie to business cases capable of attracting financing and works against special interest block grants. 4) Notes ACP funds will likely be depleted during this Congress, putting reauthorisation before the committee. 5) Raises the sharpest analytical challenge to the programme: the FCC should examine whether ACP dollars are actually driving adoption and uptake rather than subsidising service consumers would have bought anyway.
specific_asks: 1) Renew the FCC's spectrum auction authority. 2) Require the FCC to provide a mechanism for timely full-Commission review of all exercises of delegated authority. 3) Have the FCC examine the factors driving ACP adoption to ensure the dollars drive uptake rather than substituting for purchases consumers would have made anyway.
position: Federal regulator: supports auction authority renewal and procedural transparency; conditions ACP support on demonstrated additionality
verbatim_quote: "if Congress wants the program to endure, the FCC should look into the factors going into adoption and ensure that ACP dollars are driving adoption and uptake, not merely acting as a subsidy for broadband service that consumers would have purchased without such a subsidy."

hearing: “Closing the Digital Divide in Rural America”

main_arguments: 1) Testifies as Chair of the Association of Equipment Manufacturers Ag Sector Board and a vice president at AGCO, opening with his upbringing in a Texas town of fewer than 2,000 people and a family farm where ten families shared a line. 2) States plainly that despite progress the country has still not fully closed the rural divide. 3) Gives the workforce statistic: one in three of the relevant population lives and works in rural communities, against one in five overall. 4) Points to the Promoting Precision Agriculture Act as building on a recommendation from the FCC's Precision Agriculture Task Force, which the association helped create and which includes equipment manufacturers.

hearing: “Closing the Digital Divide in Rural America”

position: Fixed wireless ISP association: supports cost-effectiveness-based award criteria in USDA rural broadband programs
verbatim_quote: "Recommendations for the Next Farm Bill As you develop the 2023 Farm Bill, this Committee has an historic opportunity to lay the groundwork for achieving our shared goal of bringing connectivity to every American." | "• Base Awards on Cost Effectiveness."

hearing: “Closing the Digital Divide in Rural America”
problem_framing: Definition of 'unserved' as the contested boundary — argues ReConnect drifted into funding areas that already have service
main_arguments: 1) NCTA members operate fibre-rich networks reaching over 77% of the US population, including a growing number of rural homes; capital investment added about 6.4 million households between December 2018 and December 2021, nearly a third of them rural. 2) Makes a precise definitional charge: the original ReConnect program required at least 90% of households in a project area to be unserved, but the most recent funding round relaxed this so areas qualified even when as many as 50% of households already had broadband. 3) Argues scoring preferences should be limited to applicant experience or platform performance rather than other policy objectives. 4) Argues build-to speed requirements should retain flexibility to produce forward-leaning but cost-effective solutions.
specific_asks: 1) Restore ReConnect's focus on unserved areas and establish a common understanding of 'unserved'. 2) Direct RUS to limit scoring preferences to applicant experience or platform performance. 3) Keep performance standards flexible rather than fixing build-to speeds rigidly.
position: Cable industry association: supports narrowing eligibility to genuinely unserved areas and flexible speed standards
verbatim_quote: "While the original ReConnect program required that at least 90% of households in a project area qualify as unserved to be eligible for funding, the most recent round of funding significantly relaxed this requirement and considered areas to be eligible for funding even when as many as 50% of households already had access to broadband service."

hearing: “Closing the Digital Divide in Rural America”
problem_framing: Satellite as the economic answer where terrestrial deployment never pays — agriculture as the demonstration case
main_arguments: 1) SIA represents satellite operators, service providers, manufacturers, launch providers and ground equipment suppliers. 2) Argues satellites bring attributes terrestrial networks cannot: covering broad geographies without expensive ground infrastructure, greater resiliency, and reach into areas where terrestrial deployment remains uneconomical — at speeds and prices it claims are comparable to terrestrial alternatives. 3) Grounds the case in precision agriculture: satellite enables remote farms with livestock sensors, soil monitors and autonomous equipment far beyond terrestrial reach. 4) Supports harmonising performance targets to agricultural needs, per the Precision Ag Connectivity Task Force.
specific_asks: 1) Adopt and implement a common set of performance targets reflecting agriculture's needs. 2) Reduce bureaucratic hurdles and improve reporting for programs such as RUS, expedite licence approvals and promote interagency cooperation to facilitate satellite deployment. 3) Ensure sufficient spectrum for satellite broadband and IoT providers.
position: Satellite industry association: supports satellite eligibility and agriculture-specific performance targets in rural programs
verbatim_quote: "Satellites are capable of providing broadband and IoT to rural and remote areas of the country where it remains uneconomical for terrestrial services to deploy, and provide both speeds and prices comparable to terrestrial alternatives."

hearing: “Closing the Digital Divide in Rural America”
problem_framing: Programme continuity over novelty, with 100/100 Mbps framed as a floor rather than a target
main_arguments: 1) NTCA members deploy networks in deeply rural areas delivering services as robust and reliable as those in urban markets — parity, not adequacy, as the standard. 2) Argues against creating new initiatives that might compete or conflict with existing ones, favouring enhancing and expanding well-functioning programs to reach remaining unserved areas with service levels meeting needs over the life of the federally funded network. 3) States the speed position directly: networks built in eligible areas should meet a minimum of 100/100 Mbps, and Congress should treat 100 Mbps symmetrical as a baseline while giving USDA flexibility to raise it as use cases evolve. 4) On permitting, notes RUS can mitigate delay by letting providers seek environmental and historical review approval before an award, while asking Congress for further streamlining that preserves those protections.
specific_asks: 1) Enhance and expand existing programs rather than creating competing new initiatives. 2) Require 100/100 Mbps as the minimum build standard and treat 100 Mbps symmetrical as a baseline USDA can raise over time. 3) Streamline deployment further while preserving reasonable historical and environmental protections.
position: Rural carrier association: supports symmetrical high-speed build standards and continuity of existing USDA programs
verbatim_quote: "if anything, Congress should view the 100 Mbps symmetrical threshold as a baseline, and give USDA the flexibility to increase this standard over time as needs and use cases for broadband evolve." | "100/100 Mbps should be considered the minimum of what to build."

hearing: “Closing the Digital Divide in Rural America”
problem_framing: Future-proof network capacity as the funding criterion, argued from the cooperative model that electrified rural America
main_arguments: 1) NRECA is the service organisation for more than 900 rural electric cooperatives serving roughly 42 million people across 48 states. 2) Establishes the institutional analogy that runs through cooperative testimony: member-owned, not-for-profit entities formed to deliver service at the lowest reasonable cost, with a longstanding commitment to the communities they serve. 3) Argues Congress must prioritise scalable, future-proof networks in any future funding rounds. 4) Acknowledges building in low-density, hard-to-reach areas is challenging, but insists networks must meet consumer demand and deliver quality service to residents regardless of whether their area is classified as unserved or underserved — an explicit challenge to the unserved/underserved boundary that governs eligibility.
specific_asks: Prioritise scalable, future-proof networks in future rounds of federal funding, ensuring quality service in low-density areas regardless of unserved/underserved classification
position: Rural electric cooperative association: supports future-proof build standards and resists eligibility drawn narrowly on unserved status
verbatim_quote: "First, Congress must prioritize scalable, future-proof networks in any future rounds of federal funding." | "Congress must prioritize networks that can meet consumer demand and ensure that residents in these areas are able to receive quality service regardless of whether they are considered unserved or underserved."

main_arguments: 1) Frames the testimony as a picture of American innovation, regained opportunity and economic alternatives, none of which is possible without what she calls the lifeblood of the industry: spectrum. 2) States the dependency plainly — Open RAN cannot be deployed and its benefits reaped without sufficient licensed spectrum, and right now there is not enough. 3) Reports adoption evidence: more than 100 networks deployed worldwide make Open RAN a viable option, and the nation's rural carriers deserve more choice. 4) Gives the security fact that makes rural vendor choice urgent: Huawei continues to service US network functions, including software updates, in rural communities.
specific_asks: Address the licensed spectrum shortfall so Open RAN can be deployed, giving rural carriers viable vendor alternatives
position: Industry coalition: supports releasing licensed spectrum as the precondition for Open RAN adoption by rural carriers
verbatim_quote: "Huawei continues to service U.S. network functions, including software updates in rural communities." | "With the deployment of more than 100 networks around the world, Open RAN is now a viable option and our Nation's rural carriers deserve more choice."

hearing: Hearings to examine spectrum and national security.
problem_framing: Commercial spectrum development and national security as complementary rather than zero-sum — with interagency process breakdown as the concern
main_arguments: 1) Rejects the framing that federal spectrum policy and national security are a zero-sum game, arguing they are complementary: attending to security protects commercial interests in spectrum, and robust commercial development promotes national security. 2) Notes America's century-long global leadership in enabling new wireless services, which practitioners call spectrum policy and most Americans simply experience through working devices. 3) Argues Congress cannot legislate technological change or economic growth, but can make both more likely by unleashing scientists, engineers, entrepreneurs and consumers. 4) Raises a process failure: NTIA recommendations to the FCC against reallocating spectrum that would interfere with security-sensitive federal users were for the first time ignored, and cabinet officials as private citizens publicly contradicted their own agencies' national security positions.
specific_asks: Four key steps Congress can take to unleash innovation and growth in spectrum (the enumerated steps fall outside the captured excerpt)
position: Think tank economist: argues commercial spectrum development and security are complementary; critical of breakdown in interagency process
verbatim_quote: "Some viewers view the two as a zero sum game. I disagree. I see the two as complementary. Attending to national security concerns protects commercial interests in spectrum, and robust commercial development to spectrum promotes American national security."

hearing: Hearings to examine spectrum and national security.
problem_framing: Wi-Fi as national security infrastructure — unlicensed spectrum defended through coexistence rather than exclusivity
main_arguments: 1) Testifies with over 30 years fostering US leadership in Wi-Fi technologies, framing the hearing as an occasion to consider Wi-Fi's role in national defence and safety. 2) First dimension: the US Wi-Fi industry has been battling Chinese interests that would obstruct Wi-Fi growth globally — the security case for unlicensed. 3) Second: Wi-Fi provides communications resilience and redundancy. 4) Third, described as its hidden strength: Wi-Fi can coexist in the same frequencies used by others, including federal and military users, without causing harmful interference — the technical claim that unlicensed use does not have to displace incumbents.
specific_asks: Not stated in the captured excerpt — the testimony argues for protecting and expanding unlicensed Wi-Fi access on security and coexistence grounds
position: Unlicensed spectrum coalition: defends Wi-Fi's share of spectrum, arguing coexistence with federal and military users
verbatim_quote: "Third, the hidden strength of Wi-Fi, its ability to coexist in the same set of spectrum frequency used by others, including Federal and military users, without causing harmful interference"

hearing: Hearings to examine spectrum and national security.
problem_framing: Dynamic spectrum sharing as an under-funded research problem, with shared spectrum already serving the underserved
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as a Notre Dame professor, policy outreach director of the NSF-funded centre for spectrum innovation, and former NSF and FCC CTO, offering an explicitly balanced perspective in a personal capacity. 2) Identifies the applications that neither cellular nor Wi-Fi serves well today — factory automation, remote oilfield monitoring, precision agriculture, community networks to serve the underserved, and indoor coverage — and notes they are increasingly moving to the shared spectrum CBRS framework for affordable deployments. 3) Frames community networks serving the underserved as an emerging vertical crucial to economic and national security, placing the equity case inside the security frame. 4) Points to the FCC Technical Advisory Council's CBRS lessons-learned recommendations and the continuing Advanced Spectrum Sharing Working Group.
specific_asks: Ensure long-term R&D into dynamic spectrum sharing is adequately and sustainably funded across industry, academia and government
position: Academic engineer: supports sustained public funding for dynamic spectrum sharing research underpinning shared-spectrum deployments
verbatim_quote: "Verticals such as factory automation, remote oilfield monitoring, precision agriculture, community networks to serve the underserved, and improved indoor coverage are just some of the emerging applications that are crucial for our economic and national security. However, these are not well-served today by either cellular or Wi-Fi and are increasingly moving to the shared spectrum CBRS framework for affordable deployments."

hearing: Where Are We Now: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996
problem_framing: Section 230 as simultaneously constitutive of the internet and destructive of democracy and mental health — with the parties disagreeing about which problem they are solving
main_arguments: 1) Argues Section 230 both facilitated the internet as we know it and produced a social media ecosystem with deleterious effects on democracy and mental health. 2) Frames the statute's twenty-six words as having self-reinforcing ramifications, such that repeal could yield positive gains with a multiplier effect. 3) Makes the diagnostic point about the debate itself: Democrats and Republicans disagree over what problem they are trying to solve — for Republicans it is content moderation, framing the impasse as definitional rather than empirical.
specific_asks: Not fully stated in the captured excerpt — the testimony argues that repeal of Section 230 would produce net gains
position: Academic: supports repeal of Section 230, arguing the parties are addressing different underlying problems
verbatim_quote: "Section 230 has both facilitated the internet as we know it and has produced a social media ecosystem that has had deleterious effects on both democracy and mental health." | "Currently, Democrats and Republicans disagree over what problem they are trying to solve."

hearing: Where Are We Now: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996
problem_framing: Section 230 as a Good Samaritan law that courts inverted — immunity granted regardless of whether platforms make good faith efforts
main_arguments: 1) Restates the statutory reading she advanced in 2021: Section 230 was enacted as a Good Samaritan law, encouraging pro-social behaviour by protecting voluntary good faith efforts to assist others. 2) It was originally conceived to reward intermediaries who take affirmative steps to restrict harmful content with immunity for those actions. 3) For nearly thirty years, however, courts have instead interpreted the law to grant immunity preemptively — that is, without regard to whether any good faith moderation occurred. 4) Notes the Supreme Court in Gonzalez declined the opportunity to correct that misreading, which places the responsibility on Congress.
specific_asks: Amend Section 230 to clarify its purpose and foreclose interpretations that render the statute incoherent
position: Legal academic and civil rights advocacy: supports statutory amendment restoring the Good Samaritan reading of Section 230
verbatim_quote: "Given that the Supreme Court in Gonzalez passed on the opportunity to correct the misreading of Section 230 that has plagued courts for decades, Congress should take up the responsibility of amending Section 230 to clarify its purpose and foreclose interpretations that render the statute incoherent."

hearing: Where Are We Now: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996

specific_asks: Not stated in the captured excerpt — the response rejects a risk-balancing frame for child abuse and exploitation rather than proposing a specific mechanism
position: Legal academic: opposes applying risk-balancing analysis to child exploitation in Section 230 reform
verbatim_quote: "This question frames the issue of §230 immunity as one of risk assessment. ... However, regarding issues of child abuse and exploitation, there should be no acceptance of a ris[k-based approach]"

hearing: Legislative Proposal to Sunset Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act
problem_framing: Section 230 as a courthouse door closed to injured users — access to justice, not speech, as the frame
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as a lawyer representing victims of catastrophic injuries caused by online platforms, whose clients are denied justice because they are locked out of the courts by what she calls an obsolete law. 2) Argues the common law precedent system is meant to promote stability, consistency and equity, and that accumulated case law has instead produced the opposite here. 3) Illustrates with a case: in April 2019 a closeted 15-year-old gay boy with autism and ADHD in a rural community fell victim to a platform's juvenile-targeting marketing. 4) Adds an economic point about legal access: low-value injury claims are not viable as a business model when litigation costs exceed what the client can recover — so immunity compounds an existing barrier. 5) Frames the division of institutional responsibility: corporations will not fix this because of greed and courts cannot because of bad accumulated case law.
specific_asks: Reform Section 230 through legislation, and enact KOSA-style requirements obliging platforms to protect children's information, disable addictive product features and allow opt-out of algorithmic recommendations
position: Plaintiffs' lawyer: supports sunsetting or reforming Section 230 to restore court access for injured users
verbatim_quote: "Through legislative reform, Congress can fix what corporations won't because of greed and court's can't because of bad accumulated case law." | "low injury are not affordable as a business model when the cost of the litigation exceeds the amount recoverable to the client."

problem_framing: The 1996 Act as a missed opportunity — the diagnosis is too much FCC discretion, with subsidies faulted for serving carriers rather than households
main_arguments: 1) Testifies as a think tank senior fellow with 34 years on communications and media policy, having worked with committee members in the early 1990s on what became the Telecommunications Act. 2) Argues the Act never lived up to expectations: America's information ecosystem remains over-regulated and subject to far too much FCC meddling with markets. 3) Locates the institutional cause in Congress's own inaction — officials can abuse authority because Congress has never restrained the agency's open-ended powers. 4) Warns against mission expansion, arguing Congress must not let the FCC become a 'Federal Artificial Intelligence Commission'. 5) On affordability, makes a distributive critique from the market-liberal side: subsidies for households needing broadband assistance should long ago have been divorced from distortionary FCC regulations that mostly benefited rural carriers — that is, support should go to households rather than through carrier programs.

verbatim_quote: "For households in need of broadband assistance, subsidies should have long ago been divorced from distortionary FCC regulations that mostly benefited rural carriers." | "Congress must not let the FCC expand its mission well beyond its traditional boundaries such that it would become a veritable “Federal Artificial Intelligence Commission.”"

hearing: The Telecommunications Act of 1996: 30 Years Later

specific_asks: 1) Restore a solid jurisdictional basis for public oversight of broadband internet access service. 2) Update broadband affordability subsidies with progressive funding for an adequate benefit. 3) Keep pricing and affordability within the FCC's assessment of whether broadband is available to everyone.
